utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. The Bench apologises for being late; it's due to circumstances beyond our control. Mr. Milovancevic, if you will please round up your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone. In order to understand the essence of the indictment, the nature and character of the alleged crimes, the conflict, and the actual situation on the ground, it might be necessary to present an explanation or a view of the defence related to the constituent nature of peoples, what this term means. The Defence contends that the statistical data from 1991 indicated that there were 561.000 Croats in the federal unit of Croatia, which itself --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs in the federal unit of Croatia, which itself had about four and a half million people. Witnesses confirmed, and I think this is something my colleagues from the Prosecution will not contest, that until 1991 the Republic of Croatia was defined under its constitution as a state of the Serb and the Croat peoples. It should also not be contestable that the new Croatian government headed by the HDZ after the multi-party elections in 1990, already in mid-1990 decided -- indicated that the constitution would be amended, and they did in fact amend it in such a way that the status of the Serb population in Croatia was changed. Now they were no longer a people, but an ethnic minority. It is necessary to explain two issues here. How is it possible for 561.000 people in a federal unit that has four and a half million people, that they have the status of a people? Is it possible to explain this, to give an answer? Because that would indicate that the Serb and the Croat population were not treated in an equal manner. 12 percent of the population is given the same status as the 88 percent of the people. The question is whether this constitutional solution was there until 1991 -- 1990 in order for the Croat people to be in an unequal position. If you don't have all the information, you could conclude that, but you have to bear in mind, Your Honours, something that my colleagues from the Prosecution are not contesting, and that is the fact that in the Second World War, between 1941 and 1945, genocide was committed against the Serb people in Croatia. We saw documents about 750.000 people that had been slaughtered. This genocide was the reason, the chief reason, why in all the constitutions in force in Croatia after the Second World War of the provision, that Serbs were also a people, a nation. Why? After the Second World War, two solutions presented themselves because it is not -- one cannot accept the genocide, the results of genocide. Either parts of Croatia with a Serb population could be cut off from Croatia, thereby reducing the Croatian territory by one-third. It was a possible solution. It would have been a just solution. But there was another solution, a just solution, that was accepted both by Serbs and Croats in Croatia, for Serbs to remain within the federal unit that was Croatia, but to be given guarantees by being given the status of a people that they would never again find themselves in the position of an ethnic minority in an independent Croatia where such a genocide could be repeated against them. Your Honours, this solution was put in place and Serbs were a people in Croatia from 1945 until 1990. The genocide against the Serbs in the so-called independent state of Croatia between 1941 and 1945 was committed in a fascist creation that was recognised only by fascist states, Italy, Austria, and the Vatican. In 1941, it was recognised as an independent state of Croatia. I may have made a mistake. My colleague has just corrected me; Germany, Italy, and the Vatican. These countries created and then recognised the independent state of Croatia that then went on to commit genocide against Serbs. The first thing that happened in 1990 when the HDZ came into power was an attempt to remove this protective element for the Serbs; in other words, their status as a people. The only guarantee that these people had for their own protection was this status of a people. Why? Simply because a people has a right to decide its own fate, its status. An ethnic minority in no country in the world cannot, is not entitled to, does not have the right under international or domestic law to decide its own fate. An ethnic minority cannot say, Well, we don't want to be in Croatia anymore. But Serbs, until 1990, they did have the status of a people. Out of fear of any future genocide, they had the right enshrined in the constitution to say, No, we don't want to be in an independent Croatia. This is the very essence to the right of self-determination, and that is the essence of the term -- of the principle of a constituent people. The question is: Why did the new government, the HDZ, already in mid-1990 remove the status of a people from the Serb people? Why? Because they knew what the reaction would be. They knew that Serbs would never want to leave Yugoslavia, where according to its constitution they were duty-bound to be loyal to its state, as were, indeed, Croats and all the other peoples. And they would not want to leave that state for a very simple reason, fear that they would again be victims of genocide. The Defence is now trying to explain to you that in December 1990 Croatia did, in fact, amend its constitution, removing Serbs from the constitution, turning them into an ethnic minority, and lo and behold, the very states that created the independent states of Croatia in 1941, Germany, Austria, Italy, and the Vatican again recognise this state that seceded as a result of an armed rebellion from Yugoslavia. So this is one important element. Let me conclude this chapter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic. Earlier you referred to Italy, Austria, and the Vatican and then you corrected yourself and said not Italy, but Germany. Now you are saying Germany, Austria again, and I think also the Vatican. Is it Austria, is it Italy? Or is it Austria, Germany? Or is it Austria, Germany, Italy, Vatican?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And if you speak of Germany, please make clear what Germany. There were two Germanys after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in 1941 when the fascist powers and the Vatican recognised the independent state of Croatia that went on to commit the genocide against Serbs, there was only Germany in existence because Austria no longer existed after the Anschluss, the annexation of Austria to Germany by Hitler. It was just one Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't give us a lesson in history. Just tell us, are you referring to is it Germany or Austria, and carry on because we don't have time now. Are you including Germany or are you including Austria with Italy and the Vatican in your argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the fact that your questions perhaps show that you are unfamiliar with the history, you asked us for an explanation. In 1941, Austria did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milovancevic, I'm asking you a simple question because you have been interchanging Austria with Germany. Just correct yourself if you are wrong, and say I'm not referring to Austria. I don't know whether it was existing or not existing and carry on. We don't have the time for this. I want you to finish. Is it Austria or Germany? Don't say to me whether I know or don't know whether Austria existed at that time or not. That's not the question I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in 1991 those were Austria, Germany, Italy, and the Vatican. Those were the sovereign states as they existed at that time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Please, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in relation to this topic of the constituent nature of a people, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, that is in 1991? The reference to Austria, Germany, Italy, and the Vatican, is it 1991 you're referring to? That's what it has on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant to say that in 1991, Austria, Germany, Italy, and the Vatican were independent subjects under international law; and then in 1992, early 1992, they recognised Croatia. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You see at page 4, line -- which is what we made me interrupt you. At line -- let's start from the line 10, you said, "The Defence is now trying to explain to you that in December 1990 Croatia did, in fact, amend its constitution, removing Serbs from the constitution, turning them into an ethnic minority, and lo and behold the very states that created the independent state of Croatia in 1941, Germany, Austria," and then the transcript here says "stall." But what I heard you say was the Vatican, "and then" - I suppose that was intended to be the Vatican - "again recognised this state that seceded as a result of an armed rebellion from Yugoslavia." I just want to find out is it the Defence contention that Germany, Austria, Italy, and the Vatican did create the state of Croatia? Is that the contention? Yes or no and then we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what becomes obvious from the evidence that we led in our case is that immediately after the armed secession and armed rebellion by Croatia was recognised, the Serb population in the territory of that state met the same fate as it did in 1941. The reasons for their being given the status of a people to protect themselves against genocide were quite justified, even in the presence of UN troops. As early as in June 1992 at Maslenica and in January 1993 at the Miljevci plateau, and then in September 1993 in the Medak pocket, and in May 1995 in Operation Flash, and in August 1995 in Operation Storm, the independent state of Croatia, in the period between 1991 until 1995, according to Mr. Gruic, Prosecution expert witness, expelled between 250 and 300.000 people. In this period in 1995, the entire population left this area. This is what I wanted to point to you -- point out to you. This is very important in order for you to understand Martic, Serbs, and the actions by the government of SAO Krajina. Another thing that is very important in this case is that the case -- the situation of the accused, Martic, of Krajina itself, and the events as they were depicted in the indictment, this is something that is very closely linked and under a great influence of the actions of the international community. In the indictment itself, in the final chapters of the indictment, the Prosecutor states that in -- between July and September, the European community mediated in the Yugoslav crisis; and at the end of 1992, it recognised the independence of Slovenia and Croatia. The indictment discusses the Vance Plan. In the course of this trial, hundreds and hundreds of documents originating from the United Nations, UNPROFOR, UNHCR, the International Red Cross, EC were exhibited. Why am I saying this, Your Honour? Because the Defence wants to put to you the very essence of its case. This was a situation where a great European state, Yugoslavia, was being broken up. In 1991, it was bigger than the United Kingdom. It had 23 million people and 256.000 square kilometres, and the fact that this country was broken up was linked with all kinds of external interests. In saying this, in mentioning Germany --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm sorry to stop you and to prolong the time that you will take in your submissions, but I'd like to get this from you. In the given circumstances where the Serbs were constitutionally now a minority, as opposed to a constituent people, in the given circumstances what is it that the Serbs did not get the opportunity to do? What would they have done in those circumstances had they been a constituent people that would have saved Mr. Martic from coming before this Court and being charged under this indictment? As yet, although following your arguments all the way through, I have not been able to understand that from you; and that's what I'd like you to pin-point for me and get down to because we haven't gotten to that stage where you have taken me there as yet. I, as a member of the Trial Chamber, would very much like to be there. I followed your arguments from the inception of the trial all the way through, but please, if you could do that for me I would be grateful. In the position where you are only a minority, what is that you were prevented from doing in the given circumstances that would have been affected the price of cheese at the end of the day, to use a colloquial term? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is only a nation, a people, only an ethnic community which has the status of a nation under the constitution. Only a nation has the right to self-determination. In this particular case, this right entailed the right of Serbs to state clearly, We do not want to leave Yugoslavia together with Croatian Croats. We want to remain in our country, Yugoslavia. And when they were transformed into ethnic minority, they were immediately, automatically, denied that right. There would have been no indictment in this case had the Prosecutor abided by the then-Yugoslav constitution and appreciated these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Point for me the reason why you say that. What are the reasons that I can look to to reach this finding at the end of the day, if necessary? This is what I'd like you to do for me. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while the old constitution was in place, the old constitution of Croatia, while it was still valid until the end of 1990, the Serbs in Croatia took certain political steps in order to voice and to implement their constitutional authorities. They said, We are an autonomy within Croatia, and we will apply Croatian laws. And SAO Krajina tied that when it was created in 1990, and it was in accordance with the then-Croatian constitution and the Yugoslav constitution and in accordance with their rights. Everything that the Serbs in Croatia did back in 1990 by creating SAO Krajina and RSK was in accordance with the Yugoslav constitution because they had the status of a constituent nation. Just as the Croatian nation within Croatia had a right to self-determination, so did the Serbs in Croatia. They had a right to self-determination because they were not Johnny-come-latelies in Croatia. That was their ethnic territory; that was their country. One-third of Croatian territory according to the UN report 23280, which is Exhibit 107, so one-third of Croatian territory is an ethnic area where the Serbs constituted either a majority or a significant minority of the population. So by having the status of a constituent nation, the Serbs were entitled to voice their will for self-determination. They did it in accordance with the constitution of Yugoslavia, constitution of Croatia, in accordance with international law; whereas, Croatia carried out an armed secession, armed rebellion, and thus denied the right of the Serbs in the end breaking up Croatia by use of weapons and doing the same to Yugoslavia, which is a crime against peace. Violence, secession of Croatia, is the mother of all -- is the mother of all causes to this. It was not a sick idea of Serb leadership to persecute other non-Serbs, torture them, expel them, and do everything else that is written in the indictment. Let me just tell you that Exhibit 236, a letter of the prime minister of SAO Krajina, Milan Babic, written on the 5th of September, 1991, written to the conference on the former Yugoslavia, which was in The Hague. It was addressed to Lord Carrington and the United Nations. This letter was put to Milan Babic and he confirmed having written it. Precisely this letter speaks to the right of self-determination. This is a document in which Mr. Babic back in 1991 said that Yugoslavia had been attacked, attacked by means of armed secession and armed rebellion of Croatia, that the regular, federal army was simply acting in accordance with the law, and that it was being attacked and its members killed, that all the Serbs want is their right to self-determination, and that they do not deny the same right to the Croats. We have to ask ourselves why is it that Mr. Babic, as an accused, despite all evidence in existence, now all of a sudden changes his story when he became a witness for the Prosecution, somebody who had achieved a plea through bargaining. This is something that you might want to look into. And I would like to continue. Now, let us go back to another factor that is important in order to understand the Martic case. There are many facts in the indictment speaking about the participation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You have finished responding to me then, and I want to thank you. Please continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Another factor that is important in order to understand everything that can be found in exhibits, especially in UN documents and in the evidence given by some UN representatives, such as, for example, McElligott is the essential involvement of the international community in the crisis in Yugoslavia and their involvement in the events which unfolded in the territory in Krajina. We are not saying this, Your Honour, in order to attempt to shift the blame on to somebody else, to accuse somebody else, no. We are saying this because these are the facts that are of crucial importance for the Trial Chamber in order for them to be able to render a just judgement. There are multiple, voluminous written exhibits speaking to this. Let me draw your attention to document introduced into evidence as Exhibit 104. Maybe previously I erroneously referred to it as Exhibit 107. No, it's Exhibit 104, and this is the report to the United Nations, number 23280, dated 11th of December, 1991. This report was written after the Geneva agreement was reached on the 23rd of November, 1991, signed by the special envoy of the UN Secretary-General Mr. Vance, the then-President of Serbia Milosevic, President of Croatia Tudjman, and Defence Minister Kadijevic. This exhibit, 104, speaks of basic principles of the activities of the UN in the territory of Yugoslavia and basic principles of Vance, the special envoy of the UN Secretary-General, and Mark Goulding, the Under-Secretary of the UN. Their approach in this document - and we referred to this document many times - is that they warned that at that time on the 11th of December, 1991, a premature recognition of certain Yugoslav republics seeking that recognition, so I'm now referring to Yugoslav republics, the report of the UN on the 11th of December, 1991, referred to these republics as Yugoslav republics; whereas, the Prosecutor claim that Croatia had been independent as of October 1991. This is quite puzzling. So this document says that a premature recognition of Yugoslav republics would represent a catastrophe for the region, for peace in the world, peace in the Balkans, and peace in Yugoslavia; and that this recognition could be given only within a comprehensive solution to the Yugoslav crisis, which is something that the UN strived for. What is interesting is that the UN Secretary-General precisely in this document warned the European community, at the time led by a Dutch Minister of Foreign Affairs Van Den Broek, that a premature recognition of secessionist republics would represent a catastrophe for the peace process and for the efforts of the United Nations. Your Honours, this is a written document dated 11th of December, 1991. Despite this warning, Germany, Italy, Austria, and the Vatican, Belgium, the Netherlands, the most important European countries recognised secessionist republics. They recognised, for example, Croatia, which at that point in time did not have control over one-third of its territory. By doing so, these countries legitimatised their interests, their strike interests in the territory of Yugoslavia. They undermined the peace operation of the United Nations in Yugoslavia by doing so, because the UN troops from that moment on did not come to the territory of Yugoslavia, rather they came to Croatia. By doing so, these countries prejudge the outcome of the political crisis; and by means of that act, these countries violated the UN charter which protected the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. And Yugoslavia at that time was the only UN member. They also violated Protocol II of the Geneva Conventions; namely, Article 3. Yesterday, we said that nobody has a right to violate territorial integrity of a country under any pretext; and by doing so, these countries became accomplices in this armed secession and armed rebellion of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I just want to remind you that for the whole of this morning I haven't heard you address any of the counts that are in the indictment; and at a particular time when I stop you, I hope that you are not going to complain that you have not been given sufficient time because you have now had far in excess of what the Prosecution had to present their argument. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is the Defence that decides what counts of indictment it is going to refer to. The Defence has a right to a defence. The trial in this case spent identical amount of time on the Prosecution case and Defence case. You are giving me this warning in the most delicate portion of the defence, as we're about to present to you our key arguments. Yesterday, you said that you did not understand the arguments of the Defence; you interrupted me. I'm now asking you to allow me to present the argument of the Defence case. Please allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I believe that you should have taken the words of Judge Moloto in the spirit in which it was intended, which was by way of guidance and certainly not to undermine or in any way prejudice the Defence case or to prevent you from putting what you consider that to be which is germane, but he was merely trying to point you and guide you in the right direction. And I, myself, am a wee bit disappointed in you because I think you could have handled it a little bit more graciously, even given your concerns that your defence should be properly placed before the Court. I think you should take it in the spirit of guidance from the Trial Chamber, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm going to prevail upon the Presiding Judge to permit you the opportunity to do that which you said you are going to do. My brothers, if they would, I would be very grateful because I'm pleading on Mr. Milovancevic's behalf. I hope Mr. Whiting will not object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your words. I fully agree with what you said. My reaction was prompted by the possibility. This is how I took the words of Judge Moloto. The possibility that the Defence could be interrupted at one point in time because we were putting arguments that are not directly linked to the indictment. This is what I was trying to prevent, and I certainly meant no disrespect in doing so. Thank you, and by your leave I would continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, but I wish to endorse the words of Judge Moloto, that it should be related to and linked to the indictment. It ought to be, but it is your decision and your discretion to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Why is it that the Defence has spent for the first time so much time on this topic? We did it because the Defence believes that all factual and legal allegations in the indictment, the construction concerning the joint criminal enterprise and the indictment, were not directed at achieving the interests of justice. They were not based on facts, on actual facts. They twisted facts and evidence. They put them upside down. And in the eyes of the Defence, such an attitude of the Prosecution has a goal of achieving some political aims which evidently have something to do with the armed destruction, break-up, of Yugoslavia, the armed secession, and everything that followed from that. We tried to address this angle through our expert Dr. Smilja Avramov. The Prosecution objected to us doing that. They also objected to us mentioning the involvement of the international community in this. I think the Bench was wrong when they sided with the Prosecution, and it was prejudicial to the Defence. However, in order to judge the real intentions of everyone who participated in the Yugoslav crisis, it is important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean the Bench was wrong when it sided with the Prosecution, and it was prejudicial to the Defence? Sided on what? Where did the Bench side with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not say that you sided with the Prosecution, but that you accepted the Prosecution's suggestion that it should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Come on, Mr. Milovancevic. Stop denying things you have said. It says here: "I think the Bench was wrong when they sided with the Prosecution." Look at page 15, line 9. Yesterday, you kept on denying things you have said, and you are now denying it again. You said: "I think the Bench was wrong when it sided with the Prosecution, and it was prejudicial to the Defence." Is that not what you said? Have you been misinterpreted? Let's correct the interpreters if they interpreted you incorrectly, but I'm reading what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, the interpreters can be corrected. I said that the Chamber accepted the standpoint of the Prosecution, that the topic of the international community did not belong in this case, and Your Honours accepted this, although the standpoint of the Defence was quite the opposite to that. I couldn't say, of course, that the Chamber sided with the Prosecution. It was improperly interpreted or perhaps I spoke imprecisely, but my meaning was what I have just explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please tell the Bench, did you speak imprecisely or were you misinterpreted? It can't be both. You've got to tell us which it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the Prosecution opposed the work of the expert, an international law professor, on throwing light on facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Milovancevic. Look, just concentrate on one thing. Don't take us back. I'm asking you about just this question, where I am saying you said: "The Bench sided" -- I think,"the Bench was wrong when they sided with the Prosecution, and it was prejudicial to the Defence." Just tell us exactly what you said at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was said, Your Honours, was that the Chamber was wrong because it adopted the standpoint of the Prosecution, which can be correct or incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We consider the standpoint of the Prosecution to be incorrect, and that is our contention. And we believe that the Chamber erred in accepting the erroneous standpoint of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did the Chamber adopt the standpoint of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the point in time, Your Honour, when the redacted text of the expert report was delivered to us, where the expert of the Defence, Dr. Smilja Avramov, had in her report redacted everything that had to do with the international community, and even the conclusions of the expert were expunged. That was your decision, not ours, and we even considered whether to use that report in the proceedings or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, that was the standpoint of the Bench. That had nothing to do with the Prosecution. That was the view of the Bench about that report. It was not adopted, the standpoint of the Prosecution. And if it was prejudicial and the Bench was wrong, it was in your right to appeal. And did you appeal, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, everything was done at the very last moment, at the end of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please. Did you appeal or didn't you appeal? If you don't agree with the view of the Bench, you appeal. If you don't appeal, you accept it. It's not for you at this late stage when you did not appeal and the time for appealing is past to come and say, We adopted that. We don't adopt anybody's position. We adopt the Bench's position. And if the Defence position happens to coincide with the Bench, that doesn't mean the Bench has adopted the Defence 's position. It just so happens to be coincidental, and so also if it's coincides with the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Another point that we attempted to prove concerns the nature of the armed conflict, the existence of an armed rebellion. The actions of the Croatian armed forces and Exhibit 402 introduced by the Prosecution through witness Agotic, 200.000 heavily armed soldiers in 1991. According to the Prosecutor, there is an armed conflict on the territory throughout the time. The Prosecutor claims that the firing on Zagreb was not justified in military terms. And our expert, Colonel Milisav Sekulic, by a decision of the Chamber, had this part of his finding expunged. All his replies on which Defence insisted, trying to deal with these topics, or eliminated from his report by a decision of the Chamber. This was highly prejudicial to us. Fortunately, there is other evidence which can to a lesser extent cover these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I am to be forgiven, but I must stop you because there is a rule of etiquette and there is a rule of practice concerning how one deals with rulings of a Trial Chamber, a Tribunal, or a Bench. The ruling having been given in the course of the trial, then counsel is bound to accept it, unless he exercises a right of appeal, a right of review, or howsoever touching and concerning that ruling or judgement, and there is a finding against the Trial Chamber. As Judge Hoepfel quite properly said -- sorry, Judge Moloto, our Presiding Judge, quite properly said: You, not having exercised that right that was open to you in the normal course of practice and procedure, then retreated as if it is abiding and all parties to the trial are bound by it. And you're not allowed to refer to it and impugn it in the course of your submissions before the Court. I say this for guidance, not to embarrass you, but it is part and parcel of the adversarial system that binds this Tribunal, and you may be unaware of that fact. You may believe because in your system you can impugn it still -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No. No, I'm saying may be that in your system you can, but it is considered highly irregular here and it could amount to a contempt. If persisted in, and I say this, if you have other submissions that would have involved impugning of a properly binding ruling of this Trial Chamber, then you should avoid the use of those submissions in that way because it's not etiquette and it's not procedural correct to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm sorry to do this, but I just so the record is clear, because there's one -- one little detail which we may have all overlooked but has been drawn to my attention. At the end of the day I don't think it changes anything, but it should be put on the record. That is that Defence did seek certification for appeal of those two decisions with respect to the Chamber's rulings on those two expert witnesses and certification was denied by the Trial Chamber; however, having said that, I don't think that changes the conclusion. In our view, it's still a binding decision by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. I stand corrected. The right to seek certification was exercised. It having been denied in the normal course of the Trial Chamber's functions and duties, then, Mr. Milovancevic, you are very much bound by it. And in future, this is the manner in which you should treat findings of any Trial Chamber, whether this one or otherwise, decisions and rulings, that is how they affect any counsel in the matter or any party to the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you, when we break at quarter past, I hope you will have finished your argument. You may proceed. You are certainly not going into the second session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept what Her Honour Judge Nosworthy said and I withdraw what I have said. But I wish to provide an explanation so as not to be misunderstood. I was trying to point to some facts. I was not trying to belittle the Chamber. In any case, I accept the words of Judge Nosworthy and I withdraw what I have said. As for my being able to finish by a quarter past 10.00, I'm afraid I will not be able to do so. We can finish in the course of the next session after the break. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence witness MM-117 confirmed that the authorities of the Republika Srpska Krajina, that the Ministry of the Interior, the Cabinet, and all organs did their very best to protect public law and order. They did everything possible to protect all people regardless of ethnicity. They did everything to cooperate with UNPROFOR, and this cooperation was good. This witness, like many others, like all Defence witnesses, confirmed that every effort was made to suppress crime, to detect the perpetrators of each and every crime. This witness confirmed that cooperation with UNPROFOR on the ground was good, and then suddenly UN reports arrived saying something different, something contrary to this. Through Exhibit 965, we see that there was a meeting between Mr. Martic and Mr. Cedric Thornberry representing the UN mission in Zagreb. In this document, which is confirmed by all other evidence, Mr. Martic, according to these minutes, addressed Mr. Thornberry and said, The Western press has committed a heinous crime against the Serbs. We are only defending ourselves. Everything has been turned topsy turvy. Why don't you do something, Mr. Thornberry, to change this. In this Exhibit 965, Mr. Thornberry responds to Mr. Martic directly and says, I understand you completely, Mr. Martic. I cannot understand how the Western media reported as they did. The fact is that the Security Council at this point in time has a little more balanced picture, mark this, and the international community is gaining a clearer picture. But I cannot pretend, says Mr. Thornberry, that they have an objective picture because they don't. Because of political propaganda, the international community is treating all Serbs in the same way. These words of Mr. Thornberry, the deputy head of the mission to Yugoslavia, did not lead to any results, and this was confirmed by another witness, Mr. Barriot, who said that he was in a situation to give up his career, although he had very bright prospects at the time. He said, I was in a situation to give up my military career because I saw on the ground that the Serbs were being demonised, and I could not conceal that truth. And Mr. Cedric Thornberry confirms the same. This document also confirms, or rather, contains Cedric Thornberry's statement, The head of the civil police, UNCIVPOL, is directly subordinate to me. He's personally subordinate to me, and he says that you have excellent cooperation; and yet some Prosecution witnesses such as McElligott turned up here denying this completely and telling a different story. Documents have turned up telling a completely different story to what was testified to by a man on the ground. In the same document, 965, dated the 14th of June, 1993, Mr. Martic tells Mr. Thornberry, We are doing everything possible to protect the population. We are not drawing any distinctions between Serbs and Croats. We are doing everything in our power to protect them from those who are imperilling them. We have a problem. When the Croatian population wants to leave the territory because of the difficult situation and when they give us a signed statement to the effect that they are leaving voluntarily, they then run to the Croatian authorities and tell a different story. So Mr. Martic says, Please, Mr. Thornberry, we don't want such departures to happen anymore without the participation of UNPROFOR. And in response to this, in document 965, Cedric Thornberry says, I understand, Mr. Martic, that you are protecting the population in exceptionally difficult circumstances. You see, Your Honours, this is the truth about what was happening on the ground. Many Defence witnesses confirmed this, many. But Mr. Cedric Thornberry speaks of the Western media who have committed a crime against the Serbs in 1993; and yet now in 2006 and 2007, the Prosecutor is using these media reports as evidence against Mr. Martic. We have seen UN documents compromising the UN completely, even UN resolutions. They compromise the UN for the reasons mentioned by Cedric Thornberry because the Security Council does not have a clear picture, because the international community was not well-informed. What does Resolution 762 of the United Nations mean? It was issued in June 1992, after the first Croatian aggression on a UN protected area at the Miljevac plateau where 40 Serbs were butchered, literally butchered and thrown in a pit. What does that resolution mean condemning both sides and containing words to the effect that the pink zones fall within the jurisdiction of Croatia. They purport to condemn the aggression, take no steps, and at the same time in the same breath reward Croatia by giving it the pink zones. Witness Kirudja said that this was not part of the UN plan, that this went beyond the provisions of the Vance Plan of the United Nations. That is how the international community behaved, and we are trying to draw attention to this; whereas, in this indictment, the Prosecutor seems to be completing the job and implementing those interests. Why do I say this, Your Honours? The peace conference on Yugoslavia was never held. This indictment is the fulfilment of the wishes of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I think again you are treading on professional misconduct here in the sense that the Prosecutor is an official, an officer of this Tribunal. He has been given instructions by the mandate of this Tribunal to do what he has to do. He's got nothing to do with perpetuating or carrying forward the actions of the United Nations or the people with UNPROFOR who were there. He's merely doing his job, like you are doing your job to defend your client. He's doing his job to prosecute a case and please stop vilifying the Prosecutor. Will you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You misunderstand me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please, just stop vilifying the Prosecutor. Carry on with your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying this for the sake of my colleague from the Prosecution. I am not being personal. I'm talking about the institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Forget about the institution. That very institution you have vilifying the institution and I am not talking about any person myself. I say the Prosecutor as you refer to him or to her in your argument is not doing what you are alleging. He's just been given a job to prosecute a case based on certain facts that have been given to him. Now, just carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let us now move on to the indictment itself. Let us see how the Prosecutor does it job, on the basis of what law and what facts. Paragraph 4 of the indictment talks about the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, indicating that the aim is to -- as regards one-third of the Croatian population and great parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina to cleanse them of non-Serb population and to annex them to a Greater Serbia. This wording, this definition of a territory where crimes allegedly happened constitutes a violation of the UN charter, because the indictment covers the period between 1990 and 1995. And in 1991 at least and until May 1992, there is not such an entity as the Republic of Croatia and there is not such an entity as the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are not entities under international law. There is only Yugoslavia. And what is happening here? In paragraph 4, we're not talking about sovereign states. The goal, the objective, of such phrasing is to hide the fact in the contention of the Defence that this is an armed rebellion to avoid the mention of Yugoslavia at all as an entity under international law and to paint these events in a completely different light. Why is the Prosecution doing this and how is it doing so? Let us turn to paragraph 6 of the indictment. I am not doing this for any reason, apart from trying to present the Defence case, which boils down to this: Martic is an innocent who has been accused. He is a refugee himself, a president of a refugee people. He's been here for four years and seven months. Despite the fact that there are facts that are contrary to everything that is stated in the indictment, in what sense? In paragraph 4, you have the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina defined as sovereign states. At that time, they do not exist. There is only Yugoslavia. And then in paragraph 6 you have a list of participants in the joint criminal enterprise. Some persons are listed here, and then it says the JNA; and then the Yugoslav army; and the Army of the Republika Srpska; the police forces; the Territorial Defence, Martic's police, as they call it; voluntary units from Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia; and other political personages, figures, from the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. So you see, this last allegation in paragraph 6 gives you an idea of the real sense of the events. This is probably a slip on the part of the Prosecution because the alleged joint criminal enterprise takes place in the territory of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia in 1990 and 1991 in the middle of an armed rebellion. We're not talking about any sovereign states such as Croatia or Slovenia, and all alleged participants in the JCE listed by name in paragraph 6 are citizens, officials, soldiers, police officers, and volunteers of the only existing sovereign entity under international law, Yugoslavia, the only country that is a member of the United Nations at that time. And they're doing nothing but exercise their duties, rights, under the constitution, under the law within their sphere. They're not doing anything in any states, Croatia, Slovenia, because they don't exist at the time. They're doing their job in the territory of Yugoslavia, under the jurisdiction of the Federal Presidency, in an effort to suppress armed rebellion under Protocol II of the 1949 Geneva Convention. This is what this is all about. This is the essence. And you see, Your Honours, why did I say this thing that I said about the Prosecution? Paragraph 4 and paragraph 6 of the indictment talk about the construction of the joint criminal enterprise. Why has this been introduced? This has been introduced by the Prosecution. And in our view, the Tribunal erred when it accepted this form of responsibility because this does not exist in the Statute. It can only be introduced by the Security Council. And what was the goal for its introduction? There are two goals. First, the enumeration of the alleged participants in the joint criminal enterprise releases the Prosecution from any obligation to prove --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please, this is something that you have told us already. You have told us this previously on yesterday or the day before. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What I did not say is that by introducing this institute of JCE, the Prosecution is released from an obligation to prove many aspects; time, place, who did what, who was in charge, what was the chain of command, the subordination, what are the horizontal links among the participants. The Prosecution does not have the obligation to prove anything once the joint criminal enterprise is there for him or for them, and the Defence then can do whatever it can do defend the accused. Why was this done? This was done in order to change the picture of the events in Yugoslavia as they unfolded, to rubber stamp an illegal act that was an illegal act of the break-up of Yugoslavia and the creation of the state of Croatia. Let me give you just one example. The Prosecution did not prosecute those responsible for Operation Flash, yet he's prosecuting Martic. Now, let us move on to paragraph 7 of the indictment. This is a description of the forms in which Martic participated in the joint criminal enterprise. It says, He participated in, as it says here, in all ways of the police force to assist in the execution of the joint criminal enterprise through the commission of crimes. This is a blank cheque in a way. This is something that the Prosecutor goes on to elaborate in the indictment, yet it is in contravention of all the evidence that has been called. Prosecution witness Kerkkanen confirmed that in 1.200 pages of documents related to the Secretariat of the Interior and he made a selection in those documents, yet he was unable to find a single document in which Martic ordered a commission of any unlawful or illegal act. Well, such a monstrous plan should rest on at least one such order. Yet, this was not the case because this was not done. And I think this would be an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and we will come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As indicated before the break, I think this must bring us to the end of the Defence submissions. The Defence has made extensive submissions, and anything that may not have been covered in oral submissions I'm sure the Bench will read on the written submissions, which are expected to be as comprehensive as they can be. We'll then ask you, Mr. Whiting, at this stage, to come up with any rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the Trial Chamber to point me to a provision in the Rules envisaging that the Trial Chamber will read the final brief and will garner from that what the Defence is supposed to present in the final -- in the closing arguments. I would like to ask the Trial Chamber not to cut short the Defence's closing argument. I asked you to allow me to do so. This is a trial day, as scheduled by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the Bench is making a ruling, and the Bench is not going to point you to any Rules in that says you will get what you get. We've given you equal time. You've had more than enough time. Now, I'm making a ruling. Please don't disturb the proceedings. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you are not allowed. I do not allow you. You are repeating yourself here, indicating that you have actually finished what you want to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just asking you to give me the floor, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not giving you the floor, Mr. Milovancevic, okay? I'm just not giving you the floor unless you want to turn this court into something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence will no longer be present in this trial, in this courtroom, in a situation where my closing argument has been cut short. I can no longer defend Mr. Martic. You have just stripped me of this right and I have no other choice than to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is your choice. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please remain in the courtroom. I urge you not to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It might be a question of respect, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will endeavour to be brief in rebuttal. I will not, of course, attempt to address everything that has been raised by counsel. To the extent that relevant matters were raised, I am confident that the Trial Chamber will scrutinise the assertions made by Defence counsel and the evidentiary support in the record for those assertions, just as it will scrutinise any of our assertions made either in our final brief or our final arguments. And, secondly, many of the arguments that have been raised by Defence counsel are arguments that we have either addressed either in our final brief or our closing submissions. So I will not go through every single assertion unless the Trial Chamber wishes me to touch on something that I have not addressed. I will address a few topics. The first is the topic of armed rebellion, which was a topic that ran through the entire Defence closing from beginning to end; that the assertion was that what happened during 1991 was an armed rebellion by Croatia against Yugoslavia and various conclusions are then drawn from that with respect to both factual conclusions but also with respect to the joint criminal enterprise and also legal conclusions with respect to the applicability of international humanitarian law, and that's what I would like to address. I would like to address both of those. First of all, with respect to this factual characterisation that what was happening, to put it in such neat terms, that it was an armed rebellion of Croatia against Yugoslavia; that's just not supported by the facts. By the spring of 1991, it was already clear that Yugoslavia, as it existed until then, was not going to survive. On March 16th, 1991, Mr. Milosevic, himself, declared on television, it's in evidence as Exhibit 979, that Yugoslavia's -- Yugoslavia has entered the last phase of its agony. In June of 1991, Mr. Milosevic told Mr. Karadzic that Croatia and Slovenia should be allowed to separate, but that the only question was that the disintegration should be -- should occur in line with our inclinations. Already, everybody understood that Yugoslavia was not going to remain, was not going to continue to exist. It was disintegrating. It was coming apart. Even the Defence expert on constitutional law, Ms. Avramov agreed by the summer of 1991 everybody understood that Yugoslavia would remain intact. And so to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say wouldn't remain or would remain?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I misspoke. Thank you, Your Honour. Would not remain intact. And so to try to characterise the events after that date and the war that occurred during the summer of 1991 and into the fall of 1991 and continued until 1995 as an armed rebellion by Croatia against Yugoslavia is simply not supported by the facts. What was happening was Yugoslavia was breaking apart, and the only issue was how it was going to break apart. And Serb leaders in Belgrade and Krajina wanted to create a state for Serbs, joining together Serb areas in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Serbia and Montenegro; and that was how they wanted it to break apart, that's what they wanted the result to be. I'm pausing because I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted you to finish your point. I will ask you a question when you finish this point, before you go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I have a number of points to make under the topic of armed rebellion, but please interrupt me at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to say what would your comment be about the fact that Articles 3 and 5 of the ICTY Statute are applicable to regardless of whether a conflict is internal or international.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that is something I will address, Your Honour, and I can address it right now. It's a little bit further down on my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it is further down, deal with it when it comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I would first like to stay with the factual matters and then I'll come to those legal matters. Moreover, long before the spring of 1991, long before it was obvious that Yugoslavia was disintegrating, Serb leaders, including the accused, Mr. Martic, in the Krajina were pursuing this vision of a separate state for Serbs. And it was pursued, and this is fully set forth in our final brief, by promoting ethnic separation, ethnic conflict. And in the Krajina, it was pursued by pursuing a purpose of -- to forcibly remove the Croatian population. Now, as a part of the argument that the Defence has made trying to portray this as an armed rebellion of Croatia against Yugoslavia, there was references right at the beginning of the Defence closing argument that it was -- that Yugoslavia and the Serbs in Krajina were regular state organs. And today the Defence indicated that everything that was happening in the Krajina was following the Croatian constitution and was lawful and everything that the Serbs were doing to organise in the Krajina were lawful steps, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Following the Croatian constitution or the Yugoslav constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think both. I think both. But I think the assertion today was that the Serbs in the Krajina, their self-organisation into the SAO - I heard an open mike - that their organisation into the SAO Krajina during 1990 and into 1991 was permitted under the old Croatian constitution and that this was pursuant to the argument that they were a constituent nation; that as a constituent nation they had the right to do those things. But the evidence, Your Honours, is that every -- that there was nothing regular about what was happening in Croatian in the SAO Krajina. In 1990 and in 1991, before -- certainly before the Croatian constitution was changed in December of 1990, there was nothing regular about what was going on. There were Defence witnesses and Prosecution witnesses that agreed on this. This was illegal arming of Serbs. There were barricades that were he reacted by Serbs which were illegal. There was the Council of National Resistance that engaged in illegal provocations. The Serb leaders, including Mr. Martic, renounced openly the authority of the Croatian authorities, of the Croatian police; that was done -- that was done in a kind of de facto, public way in August of 1990. It's in Exhibits 4 and 5, and then it was done formally in the beginning of January, 1991, on the 4th of January, 1991. There is an exhibit. I don't have the reference offhand, where the SAO Krajina formally rejects the authority of the Croatian police. There are provocations. There are statements to the press made by Mr. Martic which are not authorised, and in fact he is suspended. So to characterise what is happening in 1990 in the SAO Krajina as just regular and pursuant to law and following their rights as a constituent nation is just not supported by the evidence. The Defence also - and I'm still on the facts here, and then I will very quickly move to the law. It's the next point, actually, Your Honour - the Defence also contended yesterday that it was the JNA that was suppressing this armed rebellion in Croatia and that the TO and the police in the SAO Krajina were "loyal to the federal state" and that "they had the duty to comply with all orders of the federal state." This is at 11266 of yesterday's transcript. Now, there are two things to say about this contention, aside from what I've already said about the fact that this wasn't simply an armed rebellion of Croatia. This was Yugoslavia disintegrating and various leaders making their decisions about how it was going to disintegrate. The first thing of course is speaking about duty here rings all kinds of alarm bells, because of course I think it's beyond dispute that nobody has a duty, including the police and the Serb leaders and the Krajina, including Mr. Martic. Nobody has a duty to enter into any criminal conduct or any criminal plan. So to the extent that this is an argument that Mr. Martic was just following orders of the JNA in doing whatever he did, this of course would not be a defence to criminal conduct. Moreover, it completely turns the story on its head. The reality is not -- and the evidence is overwhelming about this. The reality is not that it was the JNA in there suppressing the rebellion and ordering the TO and the police to follow along and to comply with orders. It was just the opposite. The story here is that from August of 1990 it was the Serb leaders in the Krajina, including Mr. Martic, who were trying to pull the JNA into the conflict on their side. They were trying to get the support of Belgrade and they were trying to get the support of the JNA on their side. They were at the forefront of the conflict. Look at Exhibit 496, it's an interview of Mr. Martic from October of 1994. And he says, speaking about August of 1990, he says that his message to Belgrade was, We either need arms or the JNA to protect us. Remember that at Plitvice, after Plitvice, which occurs at the end of March 1991, Mr. Martic says - and this is Exhibit 207- he says: "We will wait to see what the army does; and if they don't do anything, our men will drive the Croatian out of here." He will take the lead. He speaks many times, many times -- he will take the lead if the army doesn't come in. There are many exhibits about the close cooperation with the JNA, the fact that they have -- that they share the same goals, the support that he is receiving and has been promised from Belgrade, from Slobodan Milosevic, in terms of support and weapons. And remember that before August of 1991, the JNA is acting as a buffer between the two sides. It is acting as a buffer between the Serbs and the Croats in conflict. Whenever there is a clash, the JNA comes in and after the fighting occurs and acts as a buffer. It's only in August of 1991 that the JNA finally gets pulled in on to the side of the Serbs, and after August of 1991 it is fully on the side -- fighting for the side of the Serbs; and that is clear in Mr. Kadijevic's book, which is Exhibit 24. So, again, in December -- even in December of 1991, this is Exhibit 917, Mr. Martic is at the Presidency session of the SFRY and he is complaining about -- he is complaining that the leaders in Belgrade are not aggressive enough; that they are willing to accept this peace plan that has been proposed, the Vance Plan. And he's says, No, we don't want that peace plan, that's not acceptable. We want war. We would rather fight. We would rather go to war; and he then, after that, is persuaded by Mr. Milosevic to accept the plan. The evidence is clear on that; and then by February of 1992, he's back again at one with the Belgrade leaders and he's praising Mr. Milosevic for all the support. So the story, as I've said, is the leaders in the -- in the Krajina are pulling in support from Belgrade and from the JNA. And at a minimum, they are all working together. There is certainly no evidence to support the notion that the TO and the police in the Krajina are simply following along what the JNA tells them to do. Now, finally, Your Honour, I'll reach that point that you raised - and I apologise for the delay - the legal issue. There are a number of legal issues. And the first is what Your Honour asked, which is do Articles 3 and 5 apply to -- I'm getting guidance. Yes. I'm going to have actual legal support to support what I'm going to say now. Articles 3 and 5 indisputable apply both to -- apply to internal armed conflicts. Article 3 offences are applicable to all armed conflicts, internal or international, and I would point, with the assistance of Ms. Valabhji, to the Galic appeals judgement, paragraph 120. Article 5 explicitly speaks of crimes committed in armed conflict, whether international or internal in character. So there's no dispute about that. The second point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that article make a distinction between a civil war and a rebellion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. What I believe the Defence is referring to - and I glean this from the citations that they've made - is to the question of whether there existed an armed conflict at the time. And the Defence counsel cited to Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions, and specifically Article 1, paragraphs 1 and 2. And the issue is not -- it's not armed rebellion versus civil war, or illegal versus legal. That's not the issue. The issue is: Is it an armed conflict? And Article 1 gives some -- Article 1, paragraph 1 gives some definition about what an armed conflict is. And this has been fully explored, and the test for an armed conflict has been set out in the Tadic judgement. And this is fully referenced and set out in our brief. And essentially the test for an armed conflict, the two considerations are: Number one, the intensity of the conflict and the degree of organisation of the parties. And what is not included, according to paragraph 2, and I think this is what Defence counsel referring to and perhaps what they mean when they say "rebellion" is, it says: "The protocol shall not apply to situations of internal disturbs and intentions such as riots, isolated and sporadic acts of violence, and other acts of a similar nature as not being armed conflicts." And that has been explored in the law, riots, banditry, isolated events. Clearly, that is not what we have here. What we -- there is overwhelming evidence, and I can't really believe that the Defence would dispute this, especially given all of the talk which - some of it was exaggerated - but all of the talks about the weapons and the preparation that the Croatian side had and the army and all of the forces that they had. As I say, they weren't exactly accurate. But nonetheless, I don't really see how they would dispute that by August of 1991, both the intensity of the conflict - of the fighting - and the degree of organisation of the two sides supports an armed conflict. And just to point to a few pieces of evidence. Again, remember that the JNA before August of 1991 is acting as a buffer when there are clashes. Implicit in that is that there are two sides fighting. There is a cease-fire at the beginning of August 1991. There's no dispute about that. Some reports, two reports went in through the cross-examination of Defence witness Djukic - and I don't have the exhibit cites, but they'll be easily found - showing violations of the cease-fire, continued fighting. There was widespread fighting in the Banija region in July of 1991 and again in September of 1991. There's fighting in Kijevo. Exhibit 491 is an interesting exhibit. It's a document, an official declaration by the RSK I believe in 1992, which sets as the beginning date of the armed conflict. It says the date the armed conflict began, 17th August 1990. Mr. Kadijevic's book, which is Exhibit 24, talks about the different phases of the armed conflict of the war. Mr. Martic himself made statements which we've cited in our closing arguments, in our final brief about fighting and about war. There is no dispute that the test is satisfied that it is an armed conflict at least by August 1991; and, therefore, as a legal matter Articles 3 and 5 indisputable apply. And whether it's a rebellion -- all the other issues about whether it's a rebellion or who started it, those all fall away. If there's an armed conflict under the test, the articles apply. The Defence makes a -- I'm sorry. Okay. The Defence makes another legal argument which I think can be touched on briefly. It was made yesterday, and it was also I think kind of referred to today, which is that the protocols prohibit an intervention by a third country -- or what they prohibit, rather, is they prohibit a third country using the protocol as a basis for intervention. But that's not at issue here; that's not what this case is about. This case is not about intervention by a third country. This is not about whether a third country used the protocol as a basis for intervention. It is simply inapplicable, and it has nothing to do with the analysis of the dispute between the Serb fighters and Serb forces in the Krajina and the JNA and from Belgrade, and the Croatian side. There is no third country there. It has nothing to do with this case. So that is a complete red herring, and it's completely inapplicable. I'm going to move on to another topic unless there are any questions about that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would that, Mr. Whiting, appropriately address counsel's arguments in respect of Article 3 and nonintervention and the issues of sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it does, because the issue of the sovereignty of Yugoslavia -- that there is no issue of the sovereignty. It is not part of this case. Nothing in this case turns on whether Yugoslavia's sovereignty was violated in any way by a third country. Whether it was or it wasn't doesn't change anything about the crimes alleged or the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I thought it had more to do with the invoking of the provisions. But, thank you, I am following your thread of argument. Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You asked us to ask a question about this topic before you move to the next one. Is there anything to be said about the jurisdiction of the Tribunal insofar as - you may pardon my understanding of it - insofar as the jurisdiction is over individuals and not over states and assuming the fact that there was a third-party state that had intervened. How would that affect the proceedings here where this Tribunal has no jurisdiction over states?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think that's correct, Your Honour. I think that in the event that there was a complaint by a state that its sovereignty had been violated by another state, and whether or not that state invoked our Protocol II or invoked some other provision, that would not properly be an issue that could be taken up by this Tribunal. That's correct. The Tribunal would not be jurisdiction over that. I suppose that's something that could be raised down the street at the ICJ. But it's certainly not an issue that could be raised here, and it's not a defence. It's not a defence to the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By individuals. That's correct. And, Your Honour, I don't know. I can't say if any state that intervened -- if any state can be said to have intervened in the conflict, invoked Protocol II, I'm not aware if they did. But if they did, that's not an issue that really has any bearing on this case in our view. The next topic I wanted to address is the topic of joint criminal enterprise. The Defence raised for the first time in this case, yesterday, the claim that joint criminal enterprise liability is not within the Statute; and, therefore, Mr. Martic cannot be convicted of that. This claim fails for several reasons. The first is the claim is procedurally waived. This is a claim, this is a challenge that should have been raised in Rule 72 motion filed after the indictment and after the supporting materials were received. Rule 72 motions require the Defence to raise any issue challenging jurisdiction. And Rule 72(D)(iv) says that that includes a motion which challenges an indictment on the ground that it does not relate to any of the violations indicated in Articles 2 through 7 of the Statute. So this is clearly something that should have been raised a long time ago. It was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're saying this was a jurisdictional issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is a jurisdictional issue, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And so also it would have been a jurisdictional issue, the question of armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because that is a factual issue. That is a factual issue, so I think that is fairly raised during the trial. And I will say one last thing about armed rebellion -- armed conflict - I'm going to call it armed conflict - and that is that the Defence, until yesterday and today, never disputed that there was an armed conflict in the region. And, in fact, I think if you'll look at questions that were asked of witnesses, it was frequently understood and talked about that there was an armed conflict in the area. There was fighting on both side. And, in fact, in the armed conflict section of our brief, in the legal part, we cite to a Defence witness who talked about the dates of the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, the point I was trying to make to you is that if in fact it was the contention from the beginning of the Defence that the amount of disturbance that took place did not amount to armed conflict, then the question of jurisdiction would arise. There is no -- this is no armed conflict, in our view, as the Defence; therefore, Article 3 and 5 would not apply. Therefore, you have no jurisdiction to hear this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's correct. It can be characterised in that sense as a jurisdictional matter; however, since there are factual predicates to it, I don't think it is something that would necessarily be waived if not raised before trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, I'll leave it at that. And on the issue of waiver, I would just point to the Trial Chamber, these are these citations are not directly on point. They are more generally about waiver, but the Celebici appeals judgement, at paragraph 640, and the Naletilic appeals judgement, at paragraph 21. Secondly, and more directly on the point, with respect to whether joint criminal enterprise is properly within the Statute, this is an issue that has been considered again and again by the Tribunal. It is squarely resolved, and it is certainly within the Statute. It's not the first time that this challenge has been made. It -- I would point the Trial Chamber to the Tadic appeals judgement, paragraphs 220, 226; the decision on Ojdanic's - I'm mispronouncing that one, for some reason I cannot pronounce that - Ojdanic's motion - one Judge here is better at pronouncing that than me - motion challenging jurisdiction on joint criminal enterprise. It's dated the 21st of May, 2003, that's at paragraph 30. In the ICTR there is a decision in Karemera. It's called Decision on Jurisdictional Appeals, Joint Criminal Enterprise, 12th of April, 2006, specifically paragraph 13. The law is clear that joint criminal enterprise is a recognised mode of liability. It wasn't added. It is an interpretation of the commission mode of liability which is explicitly within the Statute, within 7(1) of the Statute. Third, the Defence misstates the source of law that is applied at the Tribunal. It is not simply the declarations of the Security Council. It is also customary law, and for that I would point again to the Ojdanic decision of the 21st of May, 2003, at paragraph 9; and the Hadzihasanovic decision on interlocutory appeal challenging jurisdiction in relation to command responsibility, 16th of July, 2003, paragraph 44. It is customary law as well as other sources of law, for example, precedent. The final argument, just very briefly. The Defence counsel suggested today that the allegation of joint criminal enterprise essentially meant that the Prosecution did not need to prove anything, and I think that's obviously not true. We have set forth the elements that are -- that we have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt, and we believe that we have done so. The next topic, Skabrnja. The Defence made a few arguments with respect to Skabrnja, and I'll just make a few brief response. The Defence claimed that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a minute, please. I apologise. The Defence did not put any arguments concerning Skabrnja, because it wasn't allowed to. So what is the Prosecutor talking about now? We never mentioned it in our closing arguments, because you did not allow us to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite -- I don't know what the Prosecutor is about to say about Skabrnja. I'm not saying you are not rightly standing up. Let's hear what he's got to say and then you can stop it if you didn't say it. Let's see because he says you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I apologise to my learned friend. I want a ruling of the Trial Chamber, and that is your ruling because you are the Presiding Judge. It is not up to you to decide what the Prosecutor is going to say. When I haven't said anything during my closing arguments in this courtroom about Skabrnja, he has no right to raise the issue. And it is up to the Chamber to rule on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response to the objection, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to respond to very specific assertions, and I'll give the page numbers. The first assertion is at 11273 from yesterday's argument. The assertion is as follows: "On the 20th of November, 1991, Split, Zadar, Zemunik airport were all blocked." That's what I was going to -- and I was going to continue along those lines responding to specific assertions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are Split, Zadar, Zemunik equivalent to or the same thing as Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, but this was in the context of talking about Skabrnja. In the beginning of the paragraph, he says, "It's all about Skabrnja." He confirmed that, and this is Mr. Milovancevic speaking: "He confirmed that in Skabrnja the units held the line until a certain point in time." He's talking about Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're saying, it's line 11273.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Page 11273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was on --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: These are points that he raised in relation to Skabrnja, and I'm going to just respond to specific points that he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm looking at 11273. At 11273 it is written here: "He confirmed that in Skabrnja the units held the line until a certain point in time, 11.30, and then the line was pierced." This is Mr. Milovancevic speaking yesterday, and now you have referred to Skabrnja. And I rule your objection out of order, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Mr. Whiting, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the armed conflict. It was a general topic, and the issue of Skabrnja --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mentioned Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I was not addressing that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mentioned Skabrnja here. Let's hear what he's going to talk about Skabrnja. We have ruled you out of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to respond just to specific points raised by Defence counsel. He said on the 20th of November, 1991, Split, Zadar, Sibenik, and Zemunik airport were all blocked. That is not supported by the evidence.
