The evidence shows that there was a cease-fire in October, that it was proceeding smoothly. Defence witness Lakic himself said that planes were taking off from Zemunik airport in November 1991. There is no evidence that these locations were blocked on the 20th of November, 1991. The second assertion is that all - it's in the next paragraph on the same page - that use of this equipment was made impossible when all these roads were blocked. Again, the evidence is to the contrary. The evidence shows that all these roads were not blocked, that the JNA had found an alternative road to use, and the witnesses were quite consistent on this point. Finally on this topic, the Defence again made references to the testimony of Marko Miljanic, and I would just say again - it's a point we've made before, but I would just say again - that the Defence picks out selective portions of his testimony. And we would urge the Trial Chamber to read the entirety of his testimony and take it in context. What he says about what was happening in Skabrnja and what the men were doing there and what their purpose was and what actually occurred, rather than taking out of context selective portions. Moving on to Bruska, the Defence counsel, in our view, speculates that the reason that the men who went to the door, to Jasna Denona's door and knocked on the door, that the reason they announced themselves as Martic's police was to gain entry to the house. Well, first of all, this theory does not even make face -- make sense on its face. The last thing in December of 1991 that you would do if you wanted to gain entry to a house in Bruska is announce yourself as Martic's police. After all the evidence is that Martic's police had been coming to that village and harassing people for weeks before that occurred. Maybe knocking on the door and saying you're the milkman or you're the Croatian police, that might be a theory. But knocking on the door to say that you're the Martic's police to gain entry, that really makes no sense. And the evidence suggests that they actually shot their way in -- started shooting before they got into the house. The second problem with this speculation is that it overlooks the fact that Ante Marinovic testified that he saw that the men had -- were not just announcing themselves as SAO Krajina police, but that they were wearing SAO Krajina police uniforms. And this starts to go quite a long way to be a ruse to gain entry, but to put on uniforms to gain entry. The evidence in our view is really unrefuted, and there is no reasonable doubt that these are Martic's police. The Defence also made the suggestion, as odd as it may seem, that Ms. Denona was treated well by the Serbs in the hospital, which is true. She testified that that was true. She did not -- I don't think she testified that she stayed a year with Serbs, and I don't know what that was a reference to. But in any event, the suggestion that I thought was odd was that Mr. Martic should get credit for that has nothing to do with the police. And to see what Ms. Denona thought of what had happened, you only need to go to page 1299 of the transcript where Mr. Milovancevic himself asked this question: "Mrs. Denona you survived a horrific event; and apart from the fact that you were seriously wounded, ten people were killed on that occasion. Have you talked to your friends and relatives for the thoughts or motives for such a horrific act?" And her answer was: "The only explanation is because we were Croats. I don't see any other reason. Why would innocent civilians and especially I myself, I was a child basically. I was only 15 years old. Why would we be a hindrance to anybody? I don't see any other reason." By the way, Defence counsel - this is a minor point, but worth just taking a second on - Defence, yesterday, said that witness MM-78 testified about a policy of Krajina authorities to expel Croats from their homes and villages wherever they lived. In his testimony he actually said RSK -- that it was a policy of the RSK. But in the context of the testimony, it's clear that he's talking about the SAO Krajina because he's talking about 1991 and he's talking about Potkonje and Vrlika and Drnis. Defence counsel suggested that these were responses given in answers to Prosecution questions; in fact, this is what the witness testified to on cross-examination. This testimony was elicited by Defence counsel, not by the Prosecution. The next topic is Milan Babic. First of all, it's obviously the case that the Prosecution's case is not built on one single witness. Mr. Babic is an important witness. There's no disputing approximate that. But the evidence of all the witnesses and all the elements corroborated not by multiple witness testimony but by documents and by what happened on the ground and the inferences that can be drawn from that. The Defence counsel's central claim seems to be now that Mr. Babic was mentally unstable when he testified and that therefore -- and he draws from that. That's his first assertion, and he draws from that that his testimony should be disregarded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I interrupt. The translation which was given to us was emotionally unstable, which is even more narrow, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Okay. Emotionally unstable. The first point to make about this is that the Parker Commission report which the Defence counsel read from yesterday. And I hesitate -- I thought about objecting but I did not. But I will say now that that is not in evidence. That report is not in evidence. It was improper to read it and to put those facts to the Trial Chamber. And in our view it was read in a selective, misleading way. But in any event, it's not in evidence and it should be completely disregarded. There is no basis to conclude, either from anything that has been put before this Trial Chamber or from the fact that Mr. Babic committed suicide, that he was emotionally unstable in a way to make his testimony unreliable. And this argument, as I think the Trial Chamber suggested yesterday, has really already been rejected by the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber. And to the extent it's further considered by the Trial Chamber in its deliberations, it should again be rejected. There is no basis to draw that conclusion that his testimony is unreliable because he committed suicide. There is simply no connection between the two. It should be noted that it is on the record that Mr. Babic was interviewed extensively by the OTP, certainly it was in 2002, but I think it may have actually begun in 2001. He testified in the Milosevic case extensively in 2002. He provided a factual basis for his own guilty plea in 2003, and all of these things occurred before he was sentenced to 13 years' imprisonment, which is the key -- Defence counsel seems to suggest that that is where things turned for Mr. Babic, is when he was sentenced. Defence counsel, of course, was given the opportunity to point to any -- to any inconsistencies between Mr. Babic's testimony before this Trial Chamber and any of his prior interviews or prior testimonies. Defence counsel did point to some, what we say, are relatively minor inconsistencies with his OTP interview, did not point to any inconsistencies with his testimony in Milosevic, did not point to any inconsistencies to the factual basis that he provided for his guilty plea. And with respect to the inconsistencies in the OTP interview, none of those went to the core facts about the joint criminal enterprise and about Mr. Martic's responsibility. Therefore, it simply cannot be concluded that -- since it's clear that the core of his testimony, the substantial points, were consistent for years, cannot be concluded that somehow he had become mentally unstable or emotionally unstable during this trial or after he was sentenced in a way that would have any effect on his testimony, because it's -- he gave the same testimony before that happened. The Defence also points to disputes that Mr. Babic had with others to suggest that there was no joint criminal enterprise, but the fact that members of the joint criminal enterprise may have had disputes about their own power or strategies to be employed - and the Prosecution accepts that that occurred - does not undermine the evidence of the joint criminal enterprise. They agreed on this common purpose. They pursued together this common purpose. It doesn't -- doesn't change anything that they also were fighting among themselves about who was going to have more power or how they were going to achieve that common purpose. Mr. Martic himself had disputes with Frenki Simatovic and Milan Babic about power; that's clear. And it's clear, as I said earlier, that in December 1991 the Krajina Serb leaders were more aggressive in their approach than the Belgrade leaders, and that's evident if you read Exhibit 917, the Presidential session. But nonetheless, the evidence shows, despite those differences and rivalries, the evidence shows that they were achieving a common purpose. The Defence today pointed to Exhibit 236, which is a letter that Milan Babic wrote in September of 1991 to The Hague Conference, which is full of very extreme language, though unfortunately it does not necessarily stand out at the time because there's other documents like it. And the Defence asks -- and Mr. Babic was extensively cross-examined on this document if you will remember. The whole document was read to him. And after it was read to him, he was asked -- he was put the question that Defence counsel raises again today which is: "How could you say that then but say something different now?" And Mr. Babic said: "Well, that was clearly exaggerated. It was over the top." He said something different now because he recognised that his own criminal conduct. He recognised that it was exaggerated what he was saying, that it was not true. He recognised what those words were at the time. Of course he had a different perspective on them today; that only makes -- otherwise, he would not have pled guilty and taken responsibility for his crimes. I'm not quite sure what to make of that argument. Finally, on the issue of Mr. Babic, we would note that the Defence cross-examined Mr. Babic on the key points of his testimony related to the joint criminal enterprise and their defence to the joint criminal enterprise, such as it is. And I'm not going to go through that analysis now, because we have fully set it out in our filing dated the 6th of April, 2006, on our filing with respect to Mr. Babic's testimony at paragraphs 39 through 43. It's a very detailed analysis on that score, and I'd like to incorporate that, by reference, into our closing submission, that analysis that's done in those paragraphs. The next topic is fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go to the next topic on Mr. Babic, I've got a question. Mr. Babic is indicated in the indictment as an alleged participant in the joint criminal enterprise. In the Prosecution's final brief, in fact, the Prosecution at paragraph 82 stated that Mr. Milan Babic accepted the responsibility for his role in the JCE alleged in the case -- in this case. However, in discussing the plurality of persons acting in the JCE, the Prosecution did not include Milan Babic as a participant therein. I refer you to paragraphs 283 to 284 of the Prosecution's final brief where members of the joint criminal enterprise are being enumerated, and Mr. Babic's name does not appear there. Is this an oversight or is it being submitted that he's not a member now; and if so, how do you reconcile the apparent contradiction?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is just an oversight. He should be included. I apologise for that. I am grateful to Your Honour calling it to our attention. He is absolutely a member of the joint criminal enterprise; he is one of the persons. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next topic is fear. The Defence counsel asserts that the Serb leaders acted out of fear of the Croatian authorities, which Defence counsel yesterday, in an interesting choice of words, referred to as "evil" in referring to the Croatian authorities. It's at 11281. Now, there's several points to make about this. The first point is that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's just been drawn to my attention that perhaps that omission might -- oversight as it might be, it is a serious omission that you've made. You amend that orally?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we may, yes, if we could amend that paragraph to include Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The amend is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The first point to make about fear, Your Honours, is that the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have anything to say about the amendment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree to have that amended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In accepting the amendment, the Chamber just wants to raise it on the record that in fact there is evidence on the record to support that amendment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. With respect to fear, the first point to make is that the Prosecution has never made -- or certainly never intended to make and should not have been interpreted to have made the extreme claim, as Defence counsel puts it, that Serbs in Croatia had no basis for fear. Of course there were fears. Serbs were becoming a minority, numerical minority, in Croatia after having had a dominant position in Yugoslavia. There were concerns, of course, of extreme statements that were being publicised by individual Croatian -- Croats and being publicised and interpreted. There were fears about what was -- how they were going to be treated, how the state was going to be organised. It was not just Yugoslavia breaking apart, but it was also communism falling away and new parties emerging. Of course there were fears. Mr. Babic spoke about his fears that he had. What the Prosecution has contended always is that the Serb leaders exploiting these fears and exaggerated them and whipped them up for their own purposes. And this is a very real distinction. It is one thing to have fears about your future and about how the state was going to be organised and about political issues that were very important at the time. It's something completely different to start talking about regularly, again and again and again and again about Ustashas, about biological extermination, about genocide and liquidation, and this talk started very early. This started back in 1990. This kind of talk -- it is this kind of talk and this kind of exaggeration which makes co-existence impossible, which leads to separation of ethnicities, leads to ethnic hatred, to conflict, and crimes. And it was this kind of talk, as distinct from ordinary fears that groups and ethnicities had in Yugoslavia and have in other countries as well, that underpinned the commission of crimes and the pursuit of the joint criminal enterprise in this case. The Serb leaders, faced with a disintegrating Yugoslavia, faced with a new situation, they chose the path towards nationalism and extremism and ethnic conflict. They made that choice. The next point is that this argument about fear is not a defence to the joint criminal enterprise, no matter how it is articulated. Even on the Defence's own terms, even accepting the characterisations by the Defence, it is not a defence. It does not undermine in any way the joint criminal enterprise. The indictment allegation a joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove Croats to form a Serb-dominated state. If this was done because of fear, that is not a defence. The law does not disappear because there is fear. In fact, that is when the law is most important; that is why the law is there. It's easy to follow the law when there's no conflict, when there's no fear, there's no war. It is because these wars have fear and threats and nationalism, that is why the law is so important and why -- when people like Milan Martic take the responsibility of commanding forces, of commanding the police, that he also takes the responsibility of following the law. Fear simply does not allow you to embark on an illegal course of conduct, it does not allow you to set aside the law. Now, interestingly, the Defence relies on the testimony of Mr. Dzakula. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could fear prompt you to act defencively? And how would you relate it to the peculiar facts of the case that we have before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's interesting because the Defence counsel himself said this was not a case of self-defence. And even if it allows you to react -- even if you're reacting defencively to fear, even in a, let's say, non-legal sense. We're not talking about legal self-defence, but we're just talking about your acting defencively, still that does not allow you to choose a path that is illegal. It does not allow you to embark out of fear and out of defensiveness down the road of creating a state and forcibly removing the Croat population through the commission of crimes. And it couldn't be otherwise, Your Honours, because otherwise if that were permissible then we would quickly see a downward spiral in any kind of ethnic conflict. Now -- may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, please do. I had said "thank you" without my microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Interestingly the Defence relies on the testimony of Mr. Dzakula, who was our first witness, to support their assertions about Serb fears and anxieties. But we suggest -- we submit that they really missed the whole point of Mr. Dzakula's testimony, because Mr. Dzakula, on cross-examination, did talk about anxieties and fears that Serbs had in Croatia, about the new Croatian symbols, about the constitution, about Croatia moving towards independence. He did talk about that. But remember that he testified that in July of 1991, he and others started -- July of 1991, he and others started the Serbian Democratic Forum - this is at page 350 of the transcript - and the purpose of which was to -- it was an initiative to prevent war. In August of 1991, he founded the SAO Western Slavonia; the purpose, to begin negotiations with Croats. In February of 1993, he entered into the Daruvar Agreement, the purpose of which was to reach the beginning of reconciliation with the Croats. He also supported the Z-4 plan in 1995. So on re-direct I asked him to try and reconcile these things. Here he had talked about fears and anxieties that Serbs had in 1990 and 1991 about the symbols and the institution and independence, and yet he was pursuing these peaceful initiatives. And it's at page 604 and 605 in the transcript - and I would urge Your Honours to pay particular attention to this exchange. I won't read the whole thing because it's quite long - and I asked him why were you doing that if you were afraid? And he said -- part of the answer was: "We knew that both Serbs and Croats were afraid, and we knew that both Serb and Croat citizens of Croatia were held hostage to those two types of policies, which were almost identical, although opposed to each other." In order words, held hostage to extremism, nationalism. And he then later testified about -- and Defence counsel made reference to it, that he -- his parents had been -- he had direct experience with World War II, because his parents had been held in a camp during World War II; and he had relatives, I think there were brothers of his father, who had been killed. He was asked about that: What lessons did you learn from that? And he essentially said that he learned to distinguish between Croats who had committed those crimes and other Croats because his parents had been freed, or maybe it was just his father, had been freed from the camp with the assistance of Croats. So despite his direct, personal experience with those events, he himself understood that this did not mean that all Croats were Ustashas, that they were all threatening, that there was going to be genocide. He understood that there was a choice, and there was a choice between extremism and nationalism and ethnic conflict and another way. And Mr. Dzakula chose that other way. Witness MM-78, he also chose that other way. Mr. Martic, no, he did not. Mr. Babic, he did not. Mr. Milosevic, he did not. The other members of the joint criminal enterprise, they chose the path of ethnic separation, of conflict, creation of a state, and forcible removal of the Croats from that state. They chose that. It was not forced upon them; that was their choice. Defence counsel also said that Mr. Dzakula provided evidence about Croat crimes that had been committed in the Pakrac area and Western Slavonia during the fall of 1991. If you read his evidence, in particular his prior testimony, which is in evidence it's Exhibit 830, he testified -- what he in fact testified about was both Serb and Croat crimes that occurred in Western Slavonia. And, in fact, as a general matter the Serb crimes preceded the Croat crimes. And I would point to pages 10428 to 29 of Exhibit 830, and this is also confirmed by Defence witness 105 at transcript pages 10515 to 19. Your Honours, I just have a -- I think I have another, maybe, ten minutes, but it's sort of a convenient time if we -- for the break, or should I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just finish off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. It may be less than ten minutes. The final issue I wanted to talk about is one that came up today,, which is the issue at -- about the change of the constitution in December of 1990, the change of the Croatian constitution. The first is that I do not believe that the -- the way that Defence counsel characterised it, the -- that the constituent nations and the connection to World War II is something that is really on the record. I'm not aware of evidence that quite makes that neat connection between the two and isolates that. I think the story is actually more complicated than that and has to do with multi-ethnic republics existing in a federal state. In any event, I'll leave that for Your Honours to determine, whether that -- that explanation is actually in evidence. But more importantly is the question that -- that came from the Trial Chamber about what this has to do with, we say, is the price of eggs, you say the price of butter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Cheese.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Cheese. And what is the implication of the change. And that is, Your Honours, that Prosecution put to Defence witness after Defence witness. We asked every single witness who testified about this issue about the change in the constitution; Well, what did this actually mean. And in our view, that question was never really answered. And the only answer that ever emerged was that it meant that the Serbs could block Croatia from becoming independent, but that's not really -- that, for one thing, doesn't make a lot of sense and doesn't -- the implications of that don't follow. It's contradicted by the conclusions of the Badinter Commission, which are in evidence, which found that, number one, Croatia did not secede from Yugoslavia, rather, Yugoslavia disintegrated. And moreover, the rights of "self-determination of groups, of Serbs in particular, within Croatia did not mean the right to territorial sovereignty but meant the right to all rights as a minority group and as -- to be respected and recognised as a group." But more importantly to this case is that it doesn't change anything about this case. It doesn't -- it doesn't -- it has no -- it is not a defence to the joint criminal enterprise. First of all, it's impossible to believe that anything would have been different if the constitution hadn't changed. How that -- how that change in the constitution makes any difference factually to any of the events that followed is completely not established. But, secondly, even if there is that change in the constitution, which there was, it doesn't change the fact that -- it doesn't provide a defence or an excuse or a reason to embark -- for Serb leaders to embark on a joint criminal enterprise on an illegal common purpose to forcibly remove Croats in order to create a Serb-dominated state. And I would note that long before the Croatian constitution was adopted in December of 1990, the Serbs had -- Serb leaders, including Mr. Martic, had rejected Croatian authority in the SAO Krajina. And with respect to various attacks that occurred by the Croatian side after starting in 1992, that Defence counsel suggests is proof of the plan on the Croatian side. Well, those obviously post-date many of the crimes alleged in the indictment; and moreover, they are not a defence to anything in the indictment. The Serb people, the Defence counsel said again and again, were as a result of the constitution being changed, were precluded from saying that they wanted to stay with Yugoslavia, precluded from having a voice, but that's just not true. The constitution was adopted in December of 1990, but in May of 1991 -- no, I'm sorry -- yes, in May of 1991 the Serbs had a referendum, in which they stated that they wanted to stay with Yugoslavia. They had a referendum, and that referendum was adopted by a large majority of the vote. So they did have the opportunity to express their views, and Mr. Martic himself spoke about this in Exhibit 973. He made reference to this expression on the part of the Serb people. So they did, in fact, have that opportunity. Now, finally, there Defence counsel cited several times to Exhibit, I think it's 236, if I can just have a moment. No, I'm sorry, it's Exhibit 965. And this is on the theme of the role of the international community, and I'm not going to say anything about that except to this point; that a cite to this meeting with Mr. Thornberry and things that Mr. Thornberry allegedly said. And the meeting, I believe, is in -- I believe it's in 1993, but it's clear on the minutes. The first point to make is that the minutes are not official minutes. These are minutes that were prepared by the Serb side, and they were not authenticated by anybody at the trial. Nobody who was present at the meeting could say that the minutes accurately reflected what Mr. Thornberry or anybody else said at that meeting. So I think that has to be kept in mind when those minutes are read. The second thing is that Mr. Martic is said to have said the following, and it's interesting and confirms, in our view, the thesis that he was pursuing the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. He says: "It should be explained that joint life of Croats and Serbs in one state is impossible because of genocide politics of Croatia. We want to separate in two states." "We want to separate" and "joint life" is impossible. That was the goal that was being pursued in 1990 and 1991, 1992, 1993, and thereafter. A separate state. Croats will have our state, we'll have our state, and the plan included, the common purpose included the forcible removal of Croats from the Serb state. In our view, this has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt and we would ask the Trial Chamber to convict Mr. Martic of the counts in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Is that it? We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the Bench invites you, if you so wish, to come in rejoinder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Perovic will deal with two topics initially, and then I will take over from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will say right at the outset something about myself. I am a kind of person who can only be impressed by facts. I worked for many years as a judge and as a lawyer, and I tend to be impressed only by the facts, nothing else, be it in this trial or any other. I'm now referring to the armed rebellion in Croatia against the central government, the then-SFRY, which was in existence. This is a topic that my learned friend, Mr. Whiting, started his speech today. The facts are merciless, and one cannot deny them. In 1990 and 1991, the then-authorities of Croatia conducted preparations; and then in 1991, they implemented an armed rebellion against the central government in the then-existing SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your warning. In the course of 1990, the then-authorities in power in Croatia, the HDZ, conducted preparations for what was to follow in 1991. These preparations were crowned, if I may say so, by the new constitution of Croatia in December of 1990. This is the document which denied the Serbs, who had had the status of a constituent nation up to that time, the right to self-determination; that is to say, to decide on their own fate and to decide whether they were going to continue living in the then-state as it existed or whether they were going to continue their life in some newly created Croatian state. This constitution from December 1990 denied the Serbs that right, stripped them of that right. In 1991, starting with the spring of 1991 until the end of that year, the Croatian authorities in power then carried out an armed rebellion against their own state, which at that time was the only internationally recognised subject in that territory; namely, the SFRY. I'm not going to point to all of the evidence adduced to prove that. I think that this is not contentious. What is contentious, though, in my sincere view, is the position of the Prosecution; that in this particular case, this was about the disintegration of a state. I have to say that this is the first time that I come across such a view; namely, that a state can disintegrate. This is a forensic or a medical term. A corpse can't disintegrate. An organic substance can decompose or disintegrate, but I have never heard this term applied to a state. Thus, the SFRY did not disintegrate. It was broken apart as a result of internal factors acting in concert with the international community. This is what it was about. The constitution from December 1990 has been mentioned a lot here; however, I have to say that so far we have not heard why would the right of Croatians, who were a constituent nation up to that time be superior, be more significant than the right of the Serbs, the other constituent nation in Croatia, to remain in the state that existed until that time. I am convinced - and there are many pieces of evidence to support that - that these two rights were equal and should have been accorded equal weight. The conflict in 1991 broke out precisely because -- I would even say that that constitution from December of 1990 was the cause of the armed conflicts which erupted in 1991, because the Serbs realised that the fact that they were stripped of the status of constituent nation meant that they were stripped of the right to decide on their own fate as a nation. This is the only proper view of the matter. So in 1991, we had an armed putsch of the then-Croatian authorities of the central government, and this putsch or coup was aimed at violent secession; unlawful seceding of one federal unit from the federal state. This is not contentious; it's supported by facts. Arguments to the effect that the state disintegrated because it was sick, because it was running fever, or had other medical conditions fall into the domain of medicine. They cannot be applied to a state. Yugoslavia, or SFRY, existed all the way up until the spring of 1992. No other interpretation is possible. In January of 1992, this new creation, the Republic of Croatia, was recognised by some states of European Union, which is what Mr. Milovancevic spoke of, but that doesn't mean that automatically, by the mere fact that it was recognised by some members of the EU, this newly created country became an international subject, no. It acquired that status several months later when it was admitted as a member into the United Nations; that is to say, all the way up until spring of 1992 in the territory of the former Yugoslavia accepted only one international subject, which was the SFRY. What Croatian authorities did during that relevant period of time in 1991 is nothing but an armed rebellion in relation to the central federal state, the only existing state, and that is the only possible view of the matter. Now something else in relation to this. I can comprehend the dilemmas faced by my learned friend, Mr. Whiting, as to the causes that led to the Serbs having the same constitutional status as Croats, even though Serbs were a minority numerically. Mr. Whiting probably doesn't know this, but I know this because I was born in that state 60 years ago and I spent most of my life there. Such a constitutional solution was dictated precisely by the events from World War II and the genocide which is beyond dispute, the genocide against the Serbian nation committed by the independent state of Croatia, the Quisling NDH, as it was known. In order to avoid any possibility of this being repeated in 1945 and later on, Croatian constitution was drafted in such a way as to grant the status of constituent nation to Serbs, just as it was granted to Croats, even though Croats had the majority in Croatia. Such a constitutional solution guaranteed to the Serbs that what happened between 1941 and 1945 would never be repeated again. By insisting on exercising their right to self-determination, the Serbs did not disturb the legitimate request of Croats to have their own independent state. That is a legitimate right of the Croats, just as it was a legitimate right of the other constituent nation in Croatia, namely Serbs, to opt for something else and to choose to live in Yugoslavia as it existed up until that time. The right of Serbs were not less significant than the right of Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, would you agree that Mr. Martic is actually not being charged or indicted for insisting on having the right to self-determination? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not fully, Your Honour. I believe that the violent secession of Croatia is the mother cause of all other events, everything else that transpired in the following five to six years. This is what I'm speaking about. Had there been no attempt to violently secede from Croatia on the part of Croatia, there would have been no Milan Martic, there would have been no RSK, and there most likely would have been no case; this case that we have been trying for over a year. So the original cause of everything that happened in Croatia - and I mean the conflict between Serbs and Croats - are the acts of Croatian authorities and their attempt to use all means, including violent secession in order to break away from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me put the question slightly differently. Do I understand you to be saying because of the actions of Croatia, Mr. Martic and the RSK did the things that Mr. Martic today stands accused of? In other words, are you saying because of the violent actions of Croatia, Mr. Martic and the RSK was therefore justified in doing the things that are alleged in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not my opinion, of course. I do not think that Mr. Martic or anybody else from the then-SAO Krajina, and later on RSK, had a right to commit crimes only because of what Croatian authorities did. Now, as to whether they did commit crimes, and if so to which extent, this is something this Trial Chamber will have to rule upon. I do not believe that Mr. Martic is guilty on any count of the indictment, and I would add to this that his acts under the situations that were described to this Trial Chamber as well as the acts of the people of RSK could only be described as a reaction, that they were forced to act that way. This is what I wanted to say in response to the Prosecutor, and now something about the evidence of Milan Babic. It is beyond dispute that Milan Babic in September of 1991 in his letter to the then-conference on Yugoslavia in The Hague wrote what he wrote. All of us had occasion to hear or read what he wrote at the time. Testifying here, he spoke of something that is quite contradictory, absolutely contradictory to what he had written at the time. I'm drawing the attention of the Court to the fact that the letter, which was sent to the conference in The Hague in September of 1991, was written by Milan Babic as a free man, and not just any man. He was a man who held a certain post, who had a certain amount of authority. Then later on, subsequently, he claimed things that are absolutely contradictory to the content of this letter, and he did that after he had reached his plea agreement with the Prosecution. These things need to be taken into account. First of all, the circumstances under which he wrote a letter when he did it as a free man; and then the second set of circumstances, where he found himself, whether voluntarily or not, when he entered into plea agreement with the Prosecution and when he definitely expected to get something in return for his testimony. What were his expectations? What was promised to him is something that we do not know, and he is no longer here to tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In your submission, what are those contradictions, the contradictions between the content of the letter and what he said after his plea bargain. If you can just remind the Bench about those so we can bear them in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, Your Honour. In the letter sent in September 1991 to the conference in The Hague, Milan Babic explicitly speaks of the status of Serbs as minority in Croatia. He says that the Serbs in Croatia faced a very complex conditions and that the Croat authorities demonstrated violence against them. I don't want to repeat the entire content of the letter, but when he came here to testify he spoke in different terms. He accepted that the Serbs and he, as one of the leaders in the RSK, as well as other people holding offices in the RSK spread some irrational fear among the Serbs in order to turn them against Croatia and Croats. He spoke about this as well, which is completely opposite of his view expressed in the letter. In the letter, he said that it was the violence used by current Croat authorities that prompted Serbs to defend themselves, to take acts in order to ensure legitimate defence. All the differences between the letter and his testimony will -- are something that the Trial Chamber will be able to discern once they study both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You bring me back to the question I asked you a few minutes ago. You say Mr. Babic said in the letter that what the people in the RSK were doing was a reaction to the violence. Let me just. You necessarily said that the violence used by current Croat authorities that prompted Serbs to defend themselves. I asked you a few minutes ago: Are you saying that the Serbs did what they did as alleged in the indictment because of the violence of the Croats? You said no. Now you're saying this is the position of Babic as a leader, as a free man, and that is what he was trying to put to The Hague Conference. Now I'm asking you: Is that the position indeed, that in fact, because of the violence that was created, that was started by the Croats, the Serbs in the RSK did what is alleged in the indictment in self-defence, as you say here? You said they were defending themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now able to understand your question better. I will try to answer it. I never ruled out the possibility that crimes were committed by the Serb side, but I am quite sure - and this is what I stated right at the beginning of my statement - that no crimes or no acts related to the RSK would have occurred had there not been a violent secession on the part of Croatia. And, now, in this armed conflict that broke out between Serbs and Croats, there certainly were crimes committed by both sides, and I'm not trying to justify any side. But what is under this big question mark here is the responsibility of Mr. Martic himself, his responsibility for any of those crimes. I fail to see this responsibility, and the Trial Chamber of course, having considered the evidence in its entirety, will rule on this matter. When I spoke about the contradictions present in Mr. Babic's acts, it is my view that the Trial Chamber will be able to give appropriate weight to this evidence in light of these circumstances that I have just spoken about. And just two more sentences. When it comes to this witness and his evidence, he committed suicide during the -- during his own testimony. And in my view - and one doesn't need to be a medical expert; this is something that is quite obvious - he evinced a high degree of mental disturbance. I think that a person who commits suicide cannot be considered to be stable, a well-balanced person. And when this is the case, I think then logic dictates us to ask whether his testimony should be considered as valid if it was given in such a state, such a mental state. Let me add here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you add, I'm sorry to do this to you. I just want to be sure that we use consistent terms. The translation says you say, "He had a degree of mental disturbance." Did you say "mental" or did you say "emotional"? There was a correction earlier today about the two statements. Are you saying mental disturbance or are you saying emotional disturbance?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me say, I used the term "unstable," because I am a layperson when it comes to medical matters. But it seems to me that these symptoms of mental instability could be observed even by laypersons. From what I studied in forensic medicine, most suicides are mentally unstable. The fact that he committed suicide in the course of giving evidence gives me the right to think that he was mentally unstable when he gave this evidence in -- before this Court. And let me now say just one more thing. It was no -- through no fault of the Defence, because it was a force majeure. Through the suicide of this witness, we were put in a position, whether you want to admit it or not, into a position where we are, in fact, prejudiced. It's a prejudicial position for us, and I now don't want to make any objections or anything. I merely want to state that this has been to our detriment. This is what I wanted to say about this topic, and my colleague Mr. Milovancevic will deal with some other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But before you sit down, I asked you whether you used the term "emotional" or "mental." In trying to answer my question, the word "mental" in the interpretation was used several times. I ask you again, and I understand you will say that you are lay, and I understand that you are lay in medical issues. All I want to know is: Are you using the word "mental disturbance" or are you using the word "emotional disturbance?" I'm asking this simply because there was a correction earlier today, and I want to know what the position of the Defence is with respect to the state of Mr. Babic. Is it the Defence's position that they allege he was "mentally disturbed," or it the Defence's position that they accept that he was "emotionally disturbed?" Accepting that we are all lay, we haven't got any medical evidence to tell us what his status was. I accept that, but what are you is speculating?. Are you speculating on "mental disturbance" or "emotional disturbance?" Just pick one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you now grant me the right to speculate, I will now tell you that it is my belief, based on my human, professional experience that this was mental instability. So this is my speculation. I'm not a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I didn't give you the right to speculate. You speculated before I said that. If you look at page 74, line 1, you said: "The fact that he committed suicide in the course of giving evidence gives me the right to think." Now, what you think is but your opinion, so it's speculation, even before I used the word speculation. You grabbed that right before I gave it to you, if I did give it to you at all. And I don't think I did. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, but that's why I used a term that is quite general, and it's a lay term I would say. I did not go into any details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, before you sit down. On the point you have just dealt with, the issue. Now, what you are saying at the end of the day is that the evidence of Milan Babic is unreliable. It ought not to be relied upon. And a conviction on that quality evidence, given the circumstances of his death, would be unsafe. That's a rough encapsulation, but you will remember there was a response from -- or, rather, a submission from the OTP that there was corroborating evidence. This was said in answer to Judge Moloto, and it was stressed again at another point. And in answer the evidence of MM-079 and MM-03 was referred to as constituting corroborating alternative evidence or additional evidence, which the Court could safely rely on as in founding a conviction. So is there anything touching and concerning those witnesses that would prevent the Court from being able to safely rely on the evidence of those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I question the reliability of Mr. Babic's testimony from two points of view. First of all, the fact that he committed suicide in the course of giving evidence; and second, the contradiction between his previous views and the views he expressed here at trial. As regards witnesses that allegedly, as the Prosecutor would have it, confirmed the -- what Mr. Babic had testified, I would not go into their testimony in detail. My learned friend, Mr. Milovancevic will speak about them. These are witnesses MM-03 and MM-079. I have to say that I do not believe that they substantially corroborate what Mr. Babic said in court. In particular, this goes for witness MM-079. As regards witness MM-03, my colleague Mr. Milovancevic disqualified for all intents and purposes his testimony, but he will say something more about that in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In the argument in rebuttal, my learned friend from the Prosecution stated that the main reason why the crimes had been committed was the vision of a separate state, that was an aspiration on the part of the Serb people, and that the establishment of the SAO Krajina and the RSK was not in accordance with the Croatian constitution, that nothing was regular in Croatia, and that this is why crimes were committed. The Defence believes that the evidence abused leads to a contrary conclusion. Exhibit 237, a transcript between General -- the transcript of a conversation between General Spegelj, the Defence Minister, and the Police Minister -- I have to apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm sorry to do this. You're interpreted as saying that the Prosecution said that nothing was regular in Croatia. Correct me if I'm wrong, I thought he said there was nothing regular in the SAO Krajina or RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your correction, Your Honour. I wanted to emphasise this sentence. Yes, he said nothing was regular in Krajina in relation to Croatia. I may have misspoken. I was imprecise. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic. In order to follow you clearly, to what points are you now reacting, responding, at what point of the rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The very beginning rebuttal where he says that the vision of a separate state for the Serbs was created a long time before 1991 and all that the Serbs had done in order to realise this goal was irregular. This is the gist of what my learned colleague said. In this respect, the Defence would like to stress that the explicit provisions in the constitution of Croatia and Yugoslavia provided for the possibility of municipalities to be created. And the attempts on the part of the Croatian government after the 1990 elections to strip that right to self-organisation from the municipalities was the cause for the rally in Serb. We think that the -- and the contention that the aspirations of the Serbs, too, actually create their own state before 1990 turns the whole case on its head. Exhibit 237 is a transcript of a conversation between Spegelj and Boljkovac, the Defence and the Interior Ministers respectively. This is October 1990, well before any self-organisation on part of the Serbs, where he says, We will solve the Knin problem by butchering them all. This is what Spegelj says, and Boljkovac responds, The Knin problem will be solved by making it disappear. We will use our weapons. Nothing will be as it was before. Croats should know that we will create a state regardless of the cost. These are the words that are recorded in an exhibit admitted by this Court, and the question is how the Serbs, the Serb population, should react to such intentions expressed by the highest echelons of the Croatian government. Your Honours, it was not necessary for them to hear those specific words at the time. Twenty-one Defence witnesses confirmed what had been happening on the ground, and Exhibits 1013 and 1014, originating from the Amnesty International about the campaign of terror, disappearance, murders, widespread campaign all over the territory of Croatia, targeting in particular those Serbs who refused to accept Croatia's independence. At the very beginning of his closing argument, my colleague from the Prosecution quoted at least five exhibits, quoting verbatim Mr. Martic's words, and this is something that I'm not challenging, where Mr. Martic says: "And we will defend our homes and hearths." And when the Vance Plan and its acceptance are discussed, Mr. Martic said we will defend our homes, and Mr. Martic never said that the defence of one's own territory or of one's own homes also entails the destruction of Croats. As regards a comment made by my colleague from the Prosecution that the JNA, the TO, and the police cooperated or acted in concert - and the Defence's view that they were loyal to the federal state - Prosecution witness Colonel Maksic, Radislav Maksic explained in quite some detail the relative jurisdictions of the federal state of the JNA, that this was an armed rebellion, and that the territorial defence was under the JNA in the chain of command, that the police was duty-bound to take part in those actions, and witness Maksic explained that the army could not have ordered the police to take part. But it had to follow the law. It had to go to the Ministry of the Interior, ask for units to be attached to them, and meetings followed, and then it was decided for a police unit to be allowed to take part in certain military operations. It is quite interesting that for the Prosecutor it is enough to simply state that in some locations they were together, the Ministry of Defence; that is to say, the JNA, TO, and police, regardless of who composed those forces and why. The witness of the Prosecution said that in the operations of the JNA in 1991, there were cases of resubordination of all units to the units of the JNA; that is to say, all units of the TO and police were subordinated to the commander of the JNA. Witness Maksic clearly explained that the commander of the JNA unit was responsible for compliance with the law, for every act, for compliance with the discipline rules; and in case, if there were any violations or crimes committed, the commander of the unit to which police or TO were resubordinated was in charge of initiating proceedings. When asked by the Prosecutor whether the commander of the unit from which these people had come, say Territorial Defence or police, who were then resubordinated to the superior JNA unit, so when asked whether the police commander or TO commander could prosecute their own members who under the JNA command had committed crimes or allegedly committed crimes, witness Maksic said that it was impossible under the law and that it was only the commander of the unit in charge of the operation that could set this in motion, the criminal proceedings. We are not emphasising this in order to shift the blame to somebody else, no. We are simply pointing your attention to the evidence of, say, General Djukic, who said that only in the 9th Corps in the course of several months, 332 criminal complaints were filed against those who committed crimes. So I'm just trying to say that this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, but is that relevant for purposes of superior responsibility of Mr. Martic? Surely, if you accept that certain units which belonged to the department of Mr. Martic were subordinated to the JNA, the question is not whether the leader of those units could punish criminals from that unit when the JNA commander was not doing so. I understand, and in fact the JNA commander is not even here to be charged. Surely, the head of that unit, as Mr. Martic, when these units come back, he should be able to discipline them. If he gets the report from the heads of those units that these are the criminal acts that were committed by members of our unit under the command of the JNA, and this is reprehensible, Mr. Martic, can you do something about them. Was that done? You understand the distinction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand fully. Thank you for your question, Your Honour. First of all, a remark. Mr. Martic never served as commander of any unit. He was the Minister of the Interior, and he exercised his authority in accordance with the law. He had no unit under his command; that's one thing. The other thing is that witness Maksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, that was not--

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, that was not my point. I understand that he was; that's why I'm saying there is no general here. But we're taking the highest political authority, the highest political authority over the general himself, over the commander of the TO and the police units. We say: Here is the highest authority. The commanders on the ground, I can understand, they are subordinated to the JNA, but if their own members misbehave and the JNA does nothing to punish them, isn't it incumbent on them to pass the information on to Mr. Martic and say: Mr. Martic, this is what our units did from the police, punish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your question, Your Honour. I understood you. Witness Maksic, who testified for the Prosecution, explained clearly that a unit which participates in combat is under the command of the most senior JNA officer; if they comprise both the JNA, the TO, and the police. And we showed documents, exhibits here, to the effect that the commander of that unit is responsible for anything done by the members who serve under him; be they from police, TO, or JNA. Witness Maksic, who is an expert for the TO and he is an officer who hails from the General Staff, said it is only this JNA, to whom they were all subordinated, who can initiate criminal proceedings against these perpetrators. Now I'm coming to the answer of your question. He said, for example, that the commander of a unit, say commander of a police station from Benkovac, that he alone cannot criminally prosecute that person, that this is under the jurisdiction of the military court because the crime was committed in the course of an armed conflict and falls under the jurisdiction of the army. Now, I come to the rest of your question. Naturally, Mr. Martic or commander or chief of any police station under whose command a JNA member committed a crime was duty-bound to criminally prosecute that person, but only if he was informed about the crime committed. What evidence did the Prosecution adduce to prove that that was the case? We have no documents to prove this. Witness, who testified here, who was the Justice Minister and President of the Court, told us that, yes, perpetrators were criminally prosecuted. And we saw court registry books showing how many people were convicted for murders. We dealt with a lot of such cases when this witness testified, MM-90. If necessary, I can tell you what exhibit number it is, those court registry books. So my position is that every citizen, every citizen of Yugoslavia, upon learning of a crime that was committed under the law and the constitution has a duty to report that and competent organs are duty-bound to prosecute. I am emphasising this now because of another fact, which is that the Prosecution believes by applying the joint criminal enterprise principle that Mr. Martic is responsible for all of those crimes, regardless of whether he knew about them or could have known about them or could have foreseen that that was going to happen or there could have been a logical consequence of an armed conflict only because he was an alleged participant in the joint criminal enterprise. It is our position that there is no evidence to support this. Mr. Prosecutor says, when speaking of this, that Martic was in favour of cooperation with Mr. Milosevic, praised cooperation with Mr. Milosevic; whereas, Mr. Kirudja said that Mr. Milosevic, as the alleged leader of the JCE, never wanted to have Krajina in Serbia. He wanted Krajina to remain within the borders of Croatia, and the only thing he wanted was to ensure that the Serbs had all adequate rights in Croatia. Speaking of Milosevic, Mr. Kirudja also said that unlike Tudjman he was a person without any kind of ethnic prejudice, that he boasted and bragged about the fact that his state was a multi-ethnic one. This is what the Prosecutor proved through their own witness, Mr. Kirudja. What is especially important to amplify is that Mr. Kirudja corroborated this with a document, showing that the relationship between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Martic was not that of two criminals participating in joint criminal enterprise, but quite the opposite, that this was a relationship between two serious men who cooperated in complex and difficult times, abiding by the international law and implementing the decisions of the United Nations. Exhibit 764 is a document of Mr. Kirudja, dated the 10th of February, 1994. Mr. Kirudja confirmed in the courtroom - and I'm reminding you of that now - that in this document it is stated in relation to the limitations of movement of civilian police and international organisations, he said that this question arose in 1994. Because in the elections in 1994 when Mr. Martic was elected, it was Milan Babic who won the most seats in the parliament, leading the SDS and the radical party. And in this document, Mr. Kirudja writes that the plan of the radicals, who were led by Leskovac in Krajina and Mr. Babic, was to prevent the delivery of humanitarian aid, block the roads, and then make it seem that the UN was not supporting Serbs so that they could attack UNPROFOR and kick them out of Krajina; and then Mr. Kirudja says that this is precisely why Milosevic supported Martic, in order to prevent this from happening, these steps from being taken against the UN. It says in the letter verbatim: "It seems that the opposition, which is Babic and the radicals, wish to stir up the population in order to reach their political goal which is a forceful removal of soldiers from UNPA zones." And it is because of this that Milosevic supported Martic and not Babic in a recent campaign. The question is now whether Martic will be able to hold power or not. This is a very valuable document brought here by the Prosecution witness, a representative of the UN, that speaks of quite a different nature of the relationship between Milosevic and Martic. This is not a relationship that exists between two criminals, and it should be easily seen from this document. It should be clearly visible to the Prosecution. The Prosecutor says that Martic abided by the orders of the JNA and that that somehow proves the JCE. This is why, Your Honours, we keep drawing your attention to the armed rebellion. The JNA was a regular armed force of the federal government; and as witness Maksic said, Every single citizen was duty-bound to abide and comply with the regulations of the federal government and the federal armed force. You heard from many witnesses here; Defence witnesses who are educated people, decent people, who went through grueling cross-examination and were not -- were not groomed for testimony here because you would have easily seen that. And all of them told you that Mr. Martic was a man who never hated anyone, who did everything in his power to protect the population. This is also stated in a UN report 897, Exhibit 897, in which the UN states that on the 2nd of February, 1993, during the Maslenica operation, the Serb refugees, who survived and who were expelled, who had lost their loved ones, who were robbed, and so on, came to Knin and that they were enraged. They were armed and were trying to take their revenge against Croatians. This document of UNPROFOR says that the Serbian police, Martic's police, housed these people in a safe haven zone in a house that one of the witnesses here described. They, UNCIVPOL, said that this was done in a fair way and that the Croats did not complain against this; and then the Prosecution brought witnesses here MM-03 and MM-78, who, contrary to any logic, say that, Yes, they were safe there. Yes they were protected, but they were sent there in order to be expelled. This is unbelievable but true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which point in rebuttal are you addressing, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very beginning the topic of a vision of separate state for Serbs when the Prosecution said that nothing was regular on the Serb side in Croatia, and then how Mr. Martic spoke about the relationship between Mr. Martic and the JNA. I'm now showing that everything done by Mr. Martic was aimed at protecting the entire population. Another topic was addressed by my learned friend, which is the issue of armed conflict. I'm now quoting the judgement from the Galic case, where it says that there is no difference between a civil war and armed rebellion. But what has it got to do with us, Your Honours? We have to make a distinction if there is one, and there is. For the Prosecutor, of course, it doesn't matter whether it's a civil war or an armed rebellion. Perhaps it is their position, but the international law says, the Geneva Conventions say that an armed rebellion is outside of the jurisdiction of international law. And we could see until which time the sovereign Yugoslavia existed, until May of 1992. Mr. Prosecutor speaks of an armed conflict, and he says it began on the 17th of August, 1990, as a document from the government of Krajina says. It is not up to the government of Krajina to judge on when the conflict broke out. Paragraph 18 says, "During the entire time to which the indictment pertains, there existed a state of armed conflict in Croatia and Bosnia;" that means that the entire time in the area protected by the UN there was a state of armed conflict from mid-1992 until 1995. I wonder now how come this was tolerated by the United Nations if this was true. There were only acts of aggression. We enumerated five of them, five acts of aggression of Croatia against the UN safe havens, and Croatia did that as an internationally recognised state. It was an internationally recognised state from the 21st of May, 1992; and already in June of 1992, it attacked a UN safe haven at Miljevac plateau and it goes all the way to the massacre in Operation Storm. These were acts of aggression of an international subject against the United Nations, and what kind of punishment followed for this? None, whatsoever. Another thing. The time when the conflict broke out in Croatia and the time when the conflict broke out in Yugoslavia, these times are different. The rebellion in Croatia begins when the population in Croatia are armed illegally; that's in mid-1990 the preparations began and October 1993 it begins, document 1005. It's a letter by 142 members of the Zadar Secretariat of the Interior. It indicates that from mid-1990 the Croatian Minister of the Interior has been taking away the weapons from the reserve police and the police officers in the police stations only to distribute them illegally to arm the population of only one ethnic background, Croat ethnic background, in Zadar, Benkovac, and Obrovac municipalities. These when the organisation and the preparations for the armed rebellion began. The armed rebellion begins then and it ends when Croatia is admitted into the United Nations, so that's May 1992; in other words, it ends when the JNA withdrew from parts of its territory in accordance with the demands set to it in the Vance Plan by the United Nations. After that, there is no armed conflict. There is only aggression aimed at the United Nations, five such acts of aggression, including Operation Flash in Western Slavonia. And the United Nations never responded to it. They did not prevent it, they did not stop it, they did not push the troops back, force the troops out. The territories were occupied, and these territories had never been under the control of the Croatian government ever since the inception of the Croatian independent state. These were acts of aggression against UN protected areas. These were also acts that violated international agreements, in particular with Operation Storm. Because under the Zagreb Agreement signed on the 29th of March, 1994, the Republic of Serbian Krajina was recognised as a subject that could enter into such agreements. So from May 1992 until Operation Storm, until the very end, there were only acts of aggression against the UN protected areas, no armed conflict, and 700 lesser attacks in those three years, as described by our witnesses. As regards Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would be interesting to hear from the Prosecutor whether he believes that the armed conflict broke out then at the same time as it did in Croatia or whether it did break out at some other time and what happened there. Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a secessionist state, was recognised on the 6th of April, 1992, again contrary to the recommendations of the Security Council. And after that, a civil war breaks out in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this is very important. It is very important to characterise a conflict in the areas covered by the indictment. So in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was a civil war in which you had the conflict of three sides; a Croat, a Serb, Bosnian. And we perhaps put a thorn in your side during the testimony, for instance, of Mr. Loncar, expert witness, Prosecution expert witness, who showed some images. But I wanted to show you some images. I wanted to show you when you asked me why I'm showing this to you, about the nature of this conflict. This was a bloody civil war there, and this is what Defence witness Barriot spoke about when he said that Alija Izetbegovic's troops in 1994 attacked the Cazin Krajina, their own territory, their own Muslim population, simply because they were in favour of a more peaceful alternative. They were opposed to Alija Izetbegovic's jihad. Witness Barriot said that 40.000 Muslims were expelled by Alija Izetbegovic's troops to the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and the government and Martic placed at their disposals all their supplies that they had, small as they were. So this is the civil war. As far as Defence is concerned, the nature of the armed conflict is important. The armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina broke out at the precise moment when parts of the international community or the international community acting against the recommendations of the UN Secretary-General from December 1991, where it was recommended that there should be a general solution for the crisis. They recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina and then the war broke out there. Next, the Prosecutor argues that this conflict has nothing to do with Yugoslavia, that this indictment has nothing to do with Yugoslavia, that the Additional Protocols also stipulate nothing to that effect. I, and the Defence in general, we did not want anyone to be put on trial for doing what they did to Yugoslavia. This is not our argument. It is our argument that we simply wanted to prove that international factor did affect the armed conflict in Yugoslavia and that Yugoslavia -- armed rebellion in Yugoslavia and that Yugoslavia is the only internationally recognised subject from 1990 until the JNA troops withdrew from this area, in accordance with the agreement reached with the UN under the Vance Plan. And I wanted to stress one more thing. Until the deployment of the UN troops - and we saw yesterday a document that was introduced through Mr. Kirudja, a Prosecution witness - that the United Nations were given guarantees by the JNA, that they would get the territory that would be in military terms and in administrative terms well-organised. So when the UN troops were deployed in UN protected areas, Mr. Martic is no longer responsible for the safety of the population. The Minister of the Interior of Krajina is not responsible for their safety. It is the civilian police of the United Nations. The United Nations are responsible for the safety, both of the Serb and of the Croat population. UNCIVPOL was there to control the population of the local police. Document Exhibit 965, the minutes from the meeting of the deputy head of the UN mission, Mr. Cedric Thornberry and Mr. Martic from the 14th of July, 1993, you can see here that the deputy commander says that CIVPOL commander is directly subordinate to me and we cooperate well. Mr. Thornberry goes on to say, I understand it to protect Croats only under very difficult circumstances. And the only argument that the Prosecutor used in order to discredit this report, this document, which is authentic, is that it has not been authorised. And I'm asking you: How can he now complain that we have not authenticated our document or authorised our document when none of the documents that the Prosecution was using had been authorised by the Serbian side or authenticated by the Serbian side. Cedric Thornberry is saying that there is a media war against Croats -- that there is a media war against Serbs and that he cannot understand the acts by the international community. Witness Barriot says that Serbs had been vilified, and he renounced his career in order to serve the truth. There was an honourable man. Everything that was done in the territory of Krajina in relation to this basic argument proffered by the Prosecution, that everything happened way back before 1990 and that it was aimed at the Serbian secession, the justice system, the prison system, the education system, the health care system, the functioning of the police, we've seen a number of documents indicating that the police had its own organisation; its rank, its titles, salary scales. Everything was completely regular. So all this shows that this was not a parallel structure, as Babic falsely testified. It is a system that existed on the basis of Yugoslav law. The fact that Serbs used -- applied Yugoslav laws in Krajina is, according to the Prosecution, proof of the existence of a joint criminal enterprise in a situation when it is quite clear that the Republic of Croatia said on the 21st of February, 1992, that federal regulations no longer -- no, in fact, it was in 1991, 21st of February, 1991, that federal laws no longer applied in our territory. So what if the Executive Council of Krajina or whoever in the Krajina government said: We will apply the Yugoslav laws. They had no other laws to copy. They could not apply the Croatian laws. And Serb laws were -- Serbian laws were in accordance with the federal laws. This is all there is to it, nothing else. The Prosecutor's argument that the issue of the application of JCE was already ruled in the appellate stage and that the Defence had had to raise this issue before going to trial, the Prosecutor fails to look at another factor. Before we went to trial, the Tribunal has already ruled on this. So why should we file on appeal against this decision under Rule 72 when this has already been ruled on by the Appeals Chamber? But we are entitled to express our own opinion that it is actually not just for the same body to decide in the second instance on this issue. It was the Security Council that should have done so, because then it would mean that the same person is acting as a Prosecutor and as a Judge - this is a saying that we have in Serbia - because now we simply don't have a second instance. This is a single-instance court, and I don't think that the Tribunal really wants to create this impression that is engendered by such acts. It is difficult to deal with this issue when you already have some decisions in place. As regards Skabrnja, my learned colleague from the Prosecution says that Defence witness Lakic confirmed that the planes had taken off. This is just not so, Your Honour. Witness Lakic confirmed that the planes that had taken off had been fired on, that they had sustained damage, and the witnesses explained everything. It sounds a little bit ironic when Prosecution witness MM-80 drew all the routes that were blocked from Benkovac to the Zemunik airport. And it is quite ironic when he says they could have used a side road, but witness Lakic said at least 20 soldiers had been killed. So this was an armed rebellion. This is what Agotic testified about and what can be seen from Exhibit 402; 200.000 heavily armed soldiers against 20.000 JNA troops. As regards Bruska, the Prosecutor said that we speculated about the reasons why somebody might introduce themselves as a police when knocking on the door. We're not speculating. We're merely thinking. Is it logical for one that is about to commit the crime to introduce him or herself? And how would you interpret the view put forward by the Prosecutor? Would they masquerade as somebody, as the police in order to gain entry into the house? But when the Prosecutor does that, he's not speculating. He quotes from Ante Marinovic's statement, where Ante Marinovic said that they wore uniforms. This is speculation. The Prosecution must prove who these people are. You saw Exhibit 602, an order by Mr. Martic, that all those people in camouflage uniforms, all those police officers who did not have the appropriate ID cards, should be disarmed. And this is what this is all about. How many movies did we see about bandits robbing banks, killing people, in disguise, disguised as police? This is reality, and the Prosecution cannot base his case on speculations because Jasna Denona and Ante Marinovic say, Serbs gave us medical treatment, Serbs protected us, Serbs saved us. And the Prosecutor says: What does it have to do with Martic? If Martic created the climate of terror, then how is it then possible that in this climate everything functioned in such a way that these people were helped rather than hindered? I do believe that my colleague from the Prosecution is, in fact, speculating, at least a tiny bit. Thank you, Your Honours, I believe we have come to the end of our session today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say something, I have not discussed all the items, all the issues raised by the Prosecutor. I still have a couple of issues I wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can put them on paper and submit them in written form, Mr. Milovancevic, because we don't have any other sitting day now. This brings us to the end of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a proposal. Since there are no other trials today, can we then continue today and I will complete my closing arguments today orally? This is not very easy for me to do in writing. This is would not be equality of arms, because my learned colleague from the Prosecution had the opportunity to address you orally and I would like to have one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Equality of arms also means equality of time, Mr. Milovancevic. You know in this address how much time you have had in relation to the time that the Prosecution has had. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How much time do you still have? How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps 40 minutes or so, half-hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Half-hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
