utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I will try to cut this down as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you say five minutes, I can give you five minutes and we can sit now for five minutes and wrap-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I address you, Your Honours. For one, this trial has been going on for one year --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. I'll give you five minutes, if you can use those five minutes and wrap up, if not let me help you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's an appropriate solution to have five more minutes. The points have been made, they've been repeated, they have had opportunities. And I would strenuously resist or object to another opportunity to have a written submission, because that's just going to open the door to further submissions and I think we need to finish. And five more minutes is enough time to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, are you ready to finish in five minutes? Please do so. 5 to 2.00, we stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecutor brought forward an argument that even if one defends, due to fear, if one defend oneself because of fear without allowing -- I apologise. If one defends oneself due to fear, then that right to self-defence does not entail a right to commit a crime. Not a single time did anybody in the Defence say anything about the need to exercise the right of self-defence by committing crimes. The Prosecutor said, One cannot, due to some alleged self-defence, persecute population. Mr. Thornberry -- Mr. Prosecutor says that one cannot persecute population because of self-defence. Mr. Thornberry, who was the deputy commander of UN said in 1993: "I fully understand that you are doing our work under difficult circumstances and trying to protect the population." So the Prosecution has nothing to corroborate their claims. He also mentioned witness Dzakula and said that he initiated some peace proposals, but witness Dzakula, as a witness for the Prosecution, said that every peace initiative who tried to start with the Croatian side was thwarted by the Croatian side; each of them failed, even in the event in Plitvice when they were disarmed, in Borovo Selo, and the Daruvar Agreement itself. Witness MM-05 said: "What does it mean when you sign an agreement on normalisation of relations; and then contrary to your agreement, and you publish it in an amended form." This puts an end to any kind of further negotiations. Those were intentional campaigns and witness Dzakula spoke the truth, because what was happening on the highway on the eve of the 1st of May, 1995, is something that the Prosecutor himself acknowledged; that was no reason and no justification for an aggression. The Defence is very grateful to our learned friend from the Prosecution for stating in his closing arguments. When it comes to Zagreb -- just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, I didn't say anything about Zagreb in the last submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that. So under the circumstances, I have a minute and a half remaining. In our closing arguments, we were not allowed to deal with the issues that were not covered in our final brief because we opted to deal with them in our closing arguments. In our final brief, we dealt with the topics that we selected, because we wanted to deal with them properly. And we left the remaining topics for the closing arguments. In this situation, we are placed in an unequal position, and this unequal position leads to only one possible conclusion, given the evidence admitted, and that is that there are no -- that there is no valid evidence to prove that there existed in joint criminal enterprise, that there was any intention to commit crimes, that Mr. Martic, in any form or shape, participated in that. Quite the opposite. All evidence point to the fact that this is a hero, who under difficult circumstances, as evidenced by Mr. Thornberry, protected the population. I see absolutely no possibility for you to adopt any other decision than an acquittal. Speculations cannot be used to found an indictment upon them, and, consequently, they can also not be used to found a conviction on them. You have before you, or rather, because of the armed rebellion and all other circumstances I quoted, a president of a persecuted people stands before you. He is innocent, just as innocent as his people are who had been expelled from their homes 12 years ago. All those homes that you saw when you travelled, homes without windows, homes without doors, are all Serbian homes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. May I be granted three minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are granted three minutes, Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, the first indictment was issued against me for Zagreb in 1995. It was done urgently, within a time-period of 50 days without any investigation. That indictment was never handed to me. I only heard about it. This indictment stood for seven years in its original form. Had there been additional evidence, I'm sure it would have been amended. When I came here voluntarily on the 15th of May, 2002, Croatian media wrote and suggested some other issues that should perhaps be looked into when indicting Mr. Martic, and the Prosecutor naturally accepted that. And whatever was written about by the media was included in the indictment. I was accused for everything and then some, and then we heard that this was libel or slander. And I'm saying that this entire indictment against me is slanderous. Why did the Prosecutor do that? Actually, I take no offence against them. Looking at the sentence that they want me to be sentenced to, naturally, such a young Prosecutor will want to have under his belt such a significant sentence; however, this Prosecutor comes from a certain country and very frequently he emphasises before you: In my legal system, in my country. And he did this for one single purpose. He wants to show you that he comes from a powerful state, from a powerful country. And this country of his, the country to which he pledged loyalty, actively participated in the persecution of my people. And now he is here to justify the acts of his country by shifting the blame for what they did to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (redacted). I'm not surprised by this appeared and I'm not surprised by the acts of this young gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Martic. I don't think that statement you made is appropriate. What do you think, about the pants?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this was published by all the media. I don't see what's secret about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am not saying it's secret. I say it's inappropriate. It has no relevance to this case, and I'll order that it be redacted. Thank you. You may proceed. Just finish off. Your three minutes are long over.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to believe that you, ladies and gentlemen, will be able to correctly assess what transpired and adopt a just judgement. I'm not going to tell you what the judgement should be; my Defence counsel spoke about that. And, otherwise, if you follow the proposal of the Prosecutor, then it will be clear that this was the judgement rendered by his system. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I said earlier that this brings us to the end of the hearing, and there are a few things that are still outstanding which I would like to place on record so that they can be followed up. First of all, we still haven't got the transcript of the site visit, and I want to believe that we should be able to get that fairly soon. When that comes up, I hope it will be distributed amongst the parties and the Bench, and it will be taken into account when the judgement is drafted. That's the first point that's outstanding. The second point that is outstanding is the public versions of the final briefs. In their written submissions, the Prosecution indicated that they would be able to do this very soon. The Defence was silent on this point. Now, the reason for that is that references may have been in the unredacted versions to protected witnesses or victims or whatever; and to the extent that it is desirable that it is to have the proceedings as public as is possible, it would be helpful if public versions of the final briefs can be filed in due course. It shouldn't be very difficult to do this. It's just a question of deleting what you think needs to be deleted in the confidential versions and giving us a copy of the redacted version. In relation to that, I would like to hear from the parties how soon this can be done so that we put a time-limit to it. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We can get ours done by Wednesday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wednesday next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we could also do it by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, I apologise. Let's say by the end of the week. May I ask something. What does this redaction mean, the redaction of the text, so that it's entirely clear to us. Your Honours, when doing the final brief, when writing it, we made sure that we did not mention a single name of a witness who is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you made sure, there's no need to give us a redacted version. If you're sure the version you've given can go to the public without compromising the security or the safety of any of the witnesses or victims, that's fine, but that is the purpose of the redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear about the approach that we are going to take, and it may be helpful to Defence counsel. We also did not make reference to any protected witness my name to any protected witness. We are going to redact any references that might identify a witness, either references contained in exhibits or in testimony. So, for example, if there was one witness who testified about a certain event and who is easily identifiable for that reason, we may redact portions of that or any other identifying information should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this might entail a lot of work. Could we please have the deadline extended to the end of the week. If possible, we will do this my Wednesday. But I want to be sure that I will comply with the deadline, that's why I am asking it be the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For the Defence, the deadline will be Friday next week. Thank you very much. Let me say, other than those two issues, no further filings will be allowed by other party. I notice also that in this Tribunal at the time of closing argument, there is a combination of argument on the merits and argument on sentence. I note that the Defence did not argue any points on sentence. I understand that they argued for a complete acquittal, and I want to say that I hope that the omission to address the question of sentence was not an oversight on the part of the Defence, that it was deliberate, and they don't intend doing so, because we are now going to close. There's not going to be any further arguments. Having said that, let me say -- yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask something. I think that two days ago we received information concerning the admission of the transcript from the site visit and that we will be allowed to file a motion regarding that. Now you're telling us that no other motions will be allowed. Does this mean that your ruling of today supersedes what you said several days ago, that there will be no further motions concerning the site visit transcripts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were told at the beginning of this stage of the trial, on the 10th, that since the transcript from the site visit were not yet produced, that the Trial Chamber will allow both the Prosecution and the Defence to file motions upon receiving these written transcripts, if they want to file a motion, if there is reason for that. Is this still in force or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, can you refer us to the transcript where this was said, Mr. Milovancevic? Let me just be clear what it is that the Court said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the first day, at the very beginning, we discussed housekeeping matters. I cannot refer you to a page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can. It's 11173, Your Honours. It's on the 10th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: At what line, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's at the -- it's in the middle of the page. It's starting at line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, but that refers to written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I think there's -- I think there may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- a motion. That's why I'm making queries my recollection is it was written submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was our recollection as well, not a motion but a written submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Written submissions if you have any corrections to make to what is on the written thing or if you think that what's written doesn't correspond with what's on the electronic recording, yes, not motions. Okay. Is that okay, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what we said on the 10th of January was understood by me as a possibility for us to use that evidence so that the transcript of the site visit can be used by us as -- in the course of our arguments during our case, not just to give some technical corrections, whether it was transcribed properly. That is not important for me at all. What is important for me is to use what is stated in the transcript in the Defence case against Mr. Martic, and we understood this to be the position of the Trial Chamber, what to do with this since this written transcript had not been admitted into evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thanks. We hear you, Mr. Milovancevic. You make those submissions. I've got to find out where I was now. Okay. I guess that's all I wanted to talk about, except then to just say -- to thank everybody else for the conduct of the trial and to say that pursuant to Rule 87 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, I, as the Presiding Judge over this case, declare the hearing of this case closed. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.12 p.m.
